title: Jordan Love, Josh Jacobs poised to make big moves on Packers all-time leaderboards
summary: If all goes well, the Packers’ offense should put up some big numbers this year. That will, of course, mean good things for the team as a whole, but it also will mean significant leaps up the all-time statistical leaderboards for a few notable names on the Packers. Here’s how the Packers could rewrite the […]
full_text: Jordan Love, number 10 of the Green Bay Packers, throws a football during training camp at Ray Nitschke Field in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin, on August 2, 2026. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images If all goes well, the Packers’ offense should put up some big numbers this year. That will, of course, mean good things for the team as a whole, but it also will mean significant leaps up the all-time statistical leaderboards for a few notable names on the Packers. Here’s how the Packers could rewrite the record books in 2026. Passing stats Jordan Love stands to make the most meaningful mark on the Packers’ record books this year. He’s currently tied with Tobin Rote for fifth all time in passing yards with 11,535. It will take him multiple seasons to catch Lynn Dickey for fourth all time, but he’ll overtake Rote with his first completion of 2026. Let’s go ahead and knock that out on the first play of the first game. With 83 passing touchdowns to his name, Love needs just seven touchdowns to pass Rote (89) for fifth all time in passing touchdowns. If he threw 51, he’d leap past Dickey for the fourth spot. That’s not impossible, but it’d take some doing — he’d only have to throw more touchdowns than any Packers player has ever thrown in a season to make it happen. A guy can dream! Rushing stats Josh Jacobs ranks 18th in Packers history with 2,258 rushing yards. The first name on his overtake list is A.J. Dillon; Jacobs needs just 171 yards to pass the former Packers’ second round pick. How high can Jacobs climb? 1,000 yards would get him past Donny Anderson for 14th all-time, and that’s probably about the upper limit. He’d need more than 1,500 yards to jump Paul Hornung (3,711) and get into the top 10, and Aaron Rodgers currently sits at 11th with 3,466. Both are probably safe this year. However, he can make some serious noise on the all-time rushing touchdowns list. His 28 touchdowns already have him tied with Dorsey Levens and Elijah Pitts for 11th, and two scores puts him past John Brockington and Tobin Rote (29 apiece) for sole possession of ninth place. And Jacobs only climbs from there. Eight touchdowns gets him past Ted Fritsch (31), Aaron Rodgers (35), and Clark Hinkle (35) for sixth all-time, and if he can get to 10 rushing touchdowns this year, he’ll pass the great Verne Lewellen for fifth all-time. More on Jacobs and his scoring abilities later. Receiving stats Christian Watson enters 2026 as the Packers’ active leader in receiving yards, ranking 30th all time. If he notches his first 1,000 yard season, he’d pass a whole host of notable names in Packers history, including Bubba Franks, Ed West, William Henderson, Romeo Doubs, Javon Walker, Ahman Green, Jermichael Finley, and Bill Schroeder, who’s currently in possession of 18th place all time with 3,435 receiving yards. I want to call out Watson’s relationship to Doubs (at least statistically) here. Watson needs 70 catches to pass Doubs’ career total of 202 in Green Bay, but just 161 yards to surpass Doubs’ 2.424. It just goes to show the difference in what the two players offer. As a bonus, Watson’s 20 receiving touchdowns currently have him tied with Bill Schroeder and Jermichael Finley for 20th in Packers history. Three touchdowns this season not only breaks that tie, but puts him past Romeo Doubs (21), Gary Knafelc (21), and Javon Walker (22) for 20th in Packers history. Nine touchdowns has him leaping Johnny Blood (28) for 18th on the big board. Elsewhere in the world of pass catching, Tucker Kraft’s 15 touchdowns has him tied with Jayden Reed and Ron Kramer for 33rd all time. Just three more scores has him leaping notable tight ends Kramer (15), Robert Tonyan (17), Donald Lee (17), and Mark Chmura (17). Six could get him past Jermichael Finley’s career total of 20. Speaking of Finley, it’s possible that Kraft could pass Finley on both the career yardage and touchdowns leaderboards this year. He’d need a bit more than 1,200 yards to do it, but he was on pace for 1,139 last year and I’d never put it past Kraft to smash through anything. He probably won’t catch Finley’s reception total of 223 this season (he’d need 111 to do it), but again…why bet against Tucker Kraft? Sooner or later, he’s going to be the Packer’s most statistically productive tight end of all time. Why not sooner? To cap off the receiving section, Matthew Golden ranks 144th in Packers’ history with just 361 receiving yards. If he manages just 500 this year, he’ll climb all the way to 82nd. Progress! Scoring stats Scoring is much less of an important metric now than it was in earlier NFL history, but the Packers have had some notable scorers during their more than century of history, so it bears mentioning. Trey Smack is off to a shaky start so far, but he’ll make something resembling history if he makes it into the regular season. If he converts just one kick, he’ll become just the 43rd in recorded Packers history to do so, or at least history as recorded by Pro Football Reference. Two made field goals makes him a top-35 kicker in Packers history. See? The bar is low! (Please improve, Trey.) Up toward the top of the leaderboard, Josh Jacobs’ 180 career points are pretty solid for two seasons, but put him in a tie for 42nd in Packers history. However, he doesn’t need to do that much to pass some notable names. He realistically won’t get anywhere near the top 10 (Jordy Nelson is 10th with 416 points, so good luck), but he’s within striking distance of Tony Canadeo (186), Aaron Rodgers (216), and Johnny Blood (224). And if you’re scoring more than Johnny Blood? Well, that’s saying something.

title: Packers coordinators speak for 1st time during training camp
summary: The Green Bay Packers’ players won’t have another open practice until after Friday’s Family Night scrimmage at Lambeau Field, but the media did get a chance to talk to the team’s coordinators on Wednesday. For the first time during training camp, we got to hear feedback from each unit’s top coaches, rather than just from […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 13: Head coach Jonathan Gannon reacts to an officials call during a game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on October 13, 2024 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. The Packers defeated the Cardinals 34-13. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ players won’t have another open practice until after Friday’s Family Night scrimmage at Lambeau Field, but the media did get a chance to talk to the team’s coordinators on Wednesday. For the first time during training camp, we got to hear feedback from each unit’s top coaches, rather than just from head coach Matt LaFleur. Here’s your recap of the major news from today’s press conferences. Cam Achord, special teams First-year Packers special teams coordinator Cam Achord was asked how Trey Smack likes his kicks to be held. He then came off the podium and did this for almost two minutes. Enjoy. pic.twitter.com/sD6yhBbZDB — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) August 5, 2026 I’m not going to bore you guys with too much special teams talk, but Cam Achord’s breakdown of why Trey Smack prefers a different way for his holder to position the ball than the typical straight up and down every single time is worth your time. Inject this into my veins. More of this PLEASE. Jonathan Gannon, defense So far, the Packers, overall, have exceeded expectations, according to new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon. This goes for “leadership, the operation and players,” in Gannon’s words. That’s great to hear! Gannon brought up versatility a lot, in the context of almost any position group in his unit. The interior defensive linemen are playing everywhere right now. The edge rushers are even kicking inside. The safeties are being placed all over the field. He said that they have the talent in the secondary to present different looks to get into the same calls, because Xavier McKinney, Evan Williams and Javon Bullard can do so much. As far as what his defense will look like, Gannon said that “each game should look different,” not because of the Packers’ talent but because of the variance from opposing offenses from week to week. It’ll be interesting to monitor how many tools Gannon has in the toolbox early on in the season, when Green Bay doesn’t have Micah Parsons, and how that will change as his players get more time in the system and Parsons returns. Adam Stenavich, offense Offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich seemed pretty pleased with his unit, stating that backup interior offensive linemen Jager Burton (a fifth-round rookie) and Jacob Monk (a third-year fifth-round pick) have the “right mindset.” He also stated that Jordan Morgan is “our left tackle, and he’s out there to prove it to everybody,” if anyone had any questions about whether or not Morgan was going to stick outside after primarily playing guard for his first two years in the NFL. Stenavich called left tackle Morgan’s “natural spot.” On the tight end front, with all the injuries, Josh Whyle and Drake Dabney have been forced into the lineup with the starting offense a lot during camp. Stenavich stated that both have improved and that maybe no one has “improved as much as [Dabney] in the first few days.” He also called Dabney more of an in-line tight end than Whyle, who has been playing a lot of fullback in camp, though that might just be the nature of being down so many bodies at the position. Running back MarShawn Lloyd, who has only been healthy enough to play 10 regular-season snaps over two seasons after being taken in the third round, has been looking good in camp, per Steno. He’s hoping that Lloyd gets a big workload in the preseason, considering how many limited live snaps Lloyd has gotten in NFL games for a third-year player.
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: Who is Anthony Campbell? Packers newcomer making his mark
summary: In an unsettled defensive line room, an unheralded newcomer is making his mark. Anthony Campbell, a 6-foot-6, 307-pound prospect who’s spent his still-young career on the fringes of the NFL, has thrown his name in the ring as a contender for the Packers’ 53-man roster. As Javon Hargrave and Devonte Wyatt come along slowly in […]
full_text: Anthony Campbell #60 and Jaden Crumedy #63 of the Green Bay Packers greet fans while walking to practice at Ray Nitschke Field in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin, on August 2, 2026. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images In an unsettled defensive line room, an unheralded newcomer is making his mark. Anthony Campbell, a 6-foot-6, 307-pound prospect who’s spent his still-young career on the fringes of the NFL, has thrown his name in the ring as a contender for the Packers’ 53-man roster. As Javon Hargrave and Devonte Wyatt come along slowly in their recovery from injuries, Campbell has been batting passes and turning heads. To this point in camp, Campbell has used his lengthy build to swat as many as four passes over the Packers’ last three practices while also showing up big in one-on-one matchups. He went 4-0 in individual pass rushing drills yesterday, according to Pete Dougherty , beating 2025 second round pick Anthony Belton twice, 2026 fifth rounder Jager Burton once, and 2026 undrafted free agent Josh Gesky once. That’s hardly a murderer’s row, but it’s nothing to sneeze at either; they’re not All-Pros, but Belton, Burton, and Gesky are all significant pieces of the Packers’ offensive line picture. But Campbell, to this point, has barely been in the picture at all, and that’s pretty much true of everywhere he’s been in his long football journey. Even in the picture I used for this article, Campbell (number 60) is an afterthought, but it’s literally the only image of him in the databases for either Getty Images or USA Today. He can’t even get top billing over the similarly unheralded Jaden Crumedy. So who is Campbell and how did he get here? A three-star recruit out of Florida’s Bartow High School, Campbell took a meandering path to the NFL. After a high school career that had him spending time at tight end and defensive end (highlighted by a 79-yard scoop and score fumble recovery), Campbell spent two years at Independence Community College in Kansas before landing at the University of Louisiana Monroe. In two seasons for the Warhawks, Campbell appeared in 17 games, recording 13 total tackles and the lone sack of his college career. After two years in Louisiana, Campbell transferred to Miami, putting him only about four hours from where he grew up. He’d play a small rotational role for the Hurricanes, appearing in just one game in 2023 and another eight in 2024. Though he’d total just 47 snaps as a senior, 10 came as a nose tackle, perhaps a nod to his bulked-up build; he’d played at 277 pounds at UL-Monroe, but was listed at an even 300 pounds at Miami. Campbell put up solid numbers in the 2025 pre-draft process, highlighted by a 9-foot, 3-inch broad jump and a decent 40-yard dash time to go with his prodigious frame. Still, pre-draft buzz was understandably hard to come by, and Campbell projected as an undrafted free agent. Dane Brugler rated him as the 115th best defensive lineman (out of 240) in the class in the 2025 edition of The Beast. Post-draft, Campbell landed with the Seahawks after minicamp tryouts with the Vikings and Eagles and spent the 2025 preseason there, playing 23 snaps across Seattle’s three exhibition games. He signed with the Seahawks’ practice squad on September 2, 2025, only to be released a day later in a series of transactions that will be of note to Packers fans. Former Packers defensive back Shemar Jean-Charles, current Packers running back Damien Martinez and one other player were released to make way for Campbell and two others on the Seattle practice squad, only for all six players to swap places again the very next day. Now, two of the six players involved are in Green Bay — the NFL world truly is small. Campbell finally arrived in Green Bay as a part of a flurry of late-season transactions leading up to the Packers’ playoff game against the Chicago Bears, joining the practice squad as o ne of 29 roster moves in a 13-day window . He didn’t appear in that playoff game — Isaiah Neyor was the only practice squad elevation — but the Packers thought enough of him to sign him to a reserve/future deal two days after their collapse in Chicago. Now, Campbell finds himself with a chance to make some noise in a defensive line group that can use all the help it can get. Defensive line has been a weakness in Green Bay for years, and injuries up front left them perilously thin at points last season. Nobody should count on Campbell to be a star, but if he can at least be a worthwhile depth piece, that’ll be a significant help to the Packers. He’ll have competition. Beyond Wyatt and Hargrave, 2026 third-round pick Chris McClellan is the only roster lock, but fourth-year Karl Brooks and second-year Warren Brinson should be considered good bets. That’s already five roster spots accounted for, leaving Campbell to compete with second-year Nazir Stackhouse and others for a job that may not even exist. But considering what he’s survived just to get to this point, it’s hard to bet against him. He’s come out of nowhere everywhere he’s been. What’s one more unexpected run to a roster spot?
author: Jon Meerdink

title: The Packers need these rotational players to contribute in 2026
summary: The top of the Green Bay Packers’ depth chart is exciting, but it’s the backups and rotational players that could help them turn into a legitimate Super Bowl contender in 2026. Every team has star players, and while the Packers have some extremely bright ones in players like Micah Parsons, Tucker Kraft, and Jordan Love, […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers defensive end Barryn Sorrell (99) against the Washington Commanders on Thursday, September 11, 2025, at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wis. The Packers defeated the Commanders 27-18. Wm. Glasheen USA TODAY NETWORK-Wisconsin | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The top of the Green Bay Packers’ depth chart is exciting, but it’s the backups and rotational players that could help them turn into a legitimate Super Bowl contender in 2026. Every team has star players, and while the Packers have some extremely bright ones in players like Micah Parsons, Tucker Kraft, and Jordan Love, it takes all 11 players on the field at any time to find consistent success. So let’s look at a few of these depth pieces who need to have positive contributions during the year to help the Packers get their NFC North title back and become a dangerous contender. Skyy Moore Green Bay’s return units were extremely disappointing last season. Along with ranking just outside of the bottom ten in average kickoff return distance, the Packers were one of just three teams to have zero returns of 40-plus yards. As if that wasn’t bad enough, the Packers also ranked dead last on punt returns with an average return of just 5.6 yards. That’s not good enough. Skyy Moore comes into Green Bay as a proven return specialist. He averaged 11.64 yards per punt return last season while also returning a kickoff 98 yards for the San Francisco 49ers. On top of his return ability, Moore can still be an effective veteran receiver to back up the likes of Jayden Reed and Matthew Golden, as made evident by some of his one-on-one reps in practice on Tuesday. Skyy Moore in 1-on-1s today: pic.twitter.com/tasmj9iyxR — Kelly Hallinan (@kellyhals) August 4, 2026 He’s not going to be WR1 in Green Bay, but Moore’s special teams contributions alone should make him a valuable part of this roster. MarShawn Lloyd Is this finally going to be the year where we see a fully healthy MarShawn Lloyd? The former third-round pick out of USC has been plagued by injuries during his first two NFL seasons, appearing in just one game where he ran the ball six times for 15 yards. Along with nagging hamstring injuries and an ankle issue that landed him on injured reserve as a rookie, the running back also underwent an emergency appendectomy just as he was activated off of IR that same season. Lloyd has showed up to Packers training camp looking healthy, and reminded fans of the burst and speed that he brought with him from college that had the Packers taking him on Day 2 of the 2024 NFL Draft. #Packers RB MarShawn Lloyd getting in some work on the 5th training camp practice. pic.twitter.com/8AmzA1pQDg — Kyle Malzhan (@KyleMalzhan) August 3, 2026 That’s an ideal play style for a change-of-pace RB, and as long as he can stay on the field, the Packers can utilize Lloyd’s speed in a variety of ways. Barryn Sorrell Micah Parsons isn’t expected to be back for the Packers until at least Week 6, throwing a wrench in Green Bay’s pass-rush plans to start the year. That means that the rest of the Packers’ EDGEs need to step up, whether it’s Lukas Van Ness playing for an extension, Dani Dennis-Sutton trying to prove himself as a rookie, or Barryn Sorrell hoping to take a step forward after a quiet rookie year. Sorrell was a fourth-round pick out of Texas last year, appearing in 14 games and playing 206 defensive snaps. The production was modest on those reps, generating just seven pressures, seven defensive stops, and 1.5 sacks on the year. That doesn’t mean all hope is lost for the second-year EDGE. At 6-foot-4 and 260 pounds, Sorrell has ideal size out on the edge as a three-down player, and his flashes were awfully exciting last year. Barryn Sorrell is a #dawg pic.twitter.com/tTfZzzOUWe — Eli Berkovits (@BookOfEli_NFL) January 5, 2026 It needs to be a group effort from Green Bay’s EDGE room with Parsons on the PUP and Rashan Gary now in Dallas, but keep an eye on Sorrell as a potential breakout candidate early in the year.

Tork Mason/USA TODAY NETWORK-Wisconsin | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Packers’ defense seems to be making a move here in the second week of training camp. It’s tough to put too much significance on headlines alone, but the panopticon of Packers’ media seems to have really turned its attention to the defense. It’s not enough to say whether or not the defense is actually good or bad or anything like that, but it feels noteworthy that a unit still without its best player is garnering this much attention in camp. I’m preaching to the choir when I say this, but the defense absolutely has to be good this year. The Packers have invested too many resources and too much time for anything short of a high quality unit, and too much depends on it for it to slack at all. This isn’t a team that’s going to have to be carried by the defense, but the more load the defense can carry, the more the offense can experiment and try different things as it sorts out its own identity. Of course, there is the lingering possibility that the defense is looking good because the offense is falling on its face in camp. There are certainly a few questions yet unresolved on that side of the ball, but let’s take the positive angle. The Packers’ defense is earning its attention through genuinely solid play, and it augurs well for the season ahead. Fingers crossed! title: Texans extend Henry To’oTo’o, solidifying the entire starting defense through 2027
summary: One of the Houston Texans’ most underappreciated defensive contributors is staying put. NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo reported Thursday morning that linebacker Henry To’oTo’o has agreed to a two-year, $16 million contract extension, keeping him in Houston through the 2028 season. The deal includes a $1M incentive option based on performance. The former fifth-round pick was […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - JANUARY 04: Linebacker Henry To'oto'o #39 of the Houston Texans runs through smoke as he is announced as a defensive starter before the NFL game between Houston Texans and Indianapolis Colts on January 4, 2026, at NRG Stadium in Houston, TX. (Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images One of the Houston Texans’ most underappreciated defensive contributors is staying put. NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo reported Thursday morning that linebacker Henry To’oTo’o has agreed to a two-year, $16 million contract extension, keeping him in Houston through the 2028 season. The deal includes a $1M incentive option based on performance. From Inside Training Camp on @nflnetwork : #Texans LB Henry To’oTo’o gets a two-year, $16 million contract extension while I practice my glottal stop to make my @gmfb colleague Manti Te’o proud. pic.twitter.com/zDqVauTJkS — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) August 6, 2026 The former fifth-round pick was an afterthought on the roster when he was initially drafted in 2023. Stuck behind veterans, To’oTo’o slowly worked his way up the depth chart and earned a starting role the past two seasons. He posted 200 tackles and four sacks over the past two seasons. While he does receive criticism for his coverage woes, he has been extremely reliable against the run and a sure tackler in open space. The short deal keeps To’oTo’o in Houston through 2028. This contract is fairly team-friendly and maintains continuity in a linebacker room quickly overrun with injuries. For context, this deal makes him the 30th highest-paid linebacker in the NFL. A great deal for the Texans given his production and health. Compare that to Azeez Al-Shaair’s contract that’s fourth highest in the league and pays him $44.6M over the next two seasons. With the new deal, General Manager Nick Caserio has inked the entire starting defense through the 2027 season. That is an incredible financial feat given the quantity of elite talent on the roster. The only notable free agent on defense will be DT Tommy Togiai.

title: Jason La Canfora talks C.J. Stroud with NFL insiders
summary: Jason La Canfora is in a very small group of journalists who sit at the tip of the NFL news cycle spear. Along with Adam Schefter and 1 or 2 others, if these guys are unavailable, a ridiculously high percentage of NFL breaking news comes through him, usually via X (Twitter). So, when I’m alerted […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - JANUARY 11: C.J. Stroud #7 and Davis Mills #10 of the Houston Texans embrace on the field after defeating the Los Angeles Chargers 32-12 during the AFC Wild Card Playoffs at NRG Stadium on January 11, 2025 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jason La Canfora is in a very small group of journalists who sit at the tip of the NFL news cycle spear. Along with Adam Schefter and 1 or 2 others, if these guys are unavailable, a ridiculously high percentage of NFL breaking news comes through him, usually via X (Twitter). So, when I’m alerted that La Canfora did an exclusive piece for the Canadian website Casino.ca, focused on Houston Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud (and Baker Mayfield & Lamar Jackson), I sit up and take notice. For the piece, La Canfora discussed the 3 field generals with a wide range of NFL folks from scouts, to executives to general managers. While there’s no “hidden truth” any of them have that predicts the future, it does come with some solid legitimacy since these are smart, successful people paid to be smart and successful when it comes to NFL quarterbacks. Right out of the gate, one of them kicks Stroud when he’s down. An advance scout who does a lot of work in the AFC South told La Canfora, regarding CJ Stroud’s playoff performance v New England, “Houston wins that game if Davis Mills starts”. It’s hard to know for sure if Mills would have won that game due to a variety of factors that we’ll never see play out. Does Vrabel dial up a different defense based on Mills vs Stroud? Are there 1 or more Patriot defenders who have a banner game due to matching up better against Mills’ style than Strouds’? Does the Houston O-Line respond worse to Mills than Stroud? Is the stage too big for Mills the same way many feel it may have been too big for Stroud? Certainly a lot to crunch through on that one… Another interesting tidbit: It stands to reason that at least one of them [Jackson, Mayfield, Stroud] won’t be back with their current team by 2027, and possibly more. Front office executives around the NFL are watching closely to see if they might be able to land one of these accomplished passers next season, as supply never meets demand with the most important position in all of professional sports. It’s hard to argue the possibility that Stroud is no longer in H-Town if this season doesn’t bear better results than last. Especially if the fault lands at C.J.’s cleats. But it also shows the value of all 3 signal callers – if any was “trash” other teams wouldn’t be watching, hoping, praying for a chance to grab 1 of them should they land in the unemployment line after the 2026 season. Here’s where La Canfora focuses in on Stroud: Stroud, also a first-round pick, is three years into his career, they have a fifth-year option on him and they could apply franchise tags after that. The Texans were never going to make a real push to sign him this year after some dramatic declines from his rookie season, and general manager Nick Caserio is a product of Bill Belichick in New England – even Tom Brady took less to be a part of that dynasty and there was no dynasty without Brady. “Nick is no pushover,” another general manager told me this offseason. “Stroud is going to have to earn it.” The notion that Caserio and the Texans have to give Stroud a big paycheck at the end of this year isn’t necessarily rooted in fact. The option and tags could buy them time to get Stroud onboard and/or replaced. La Canfora’s hot take on how this plays out: Prediction: Stroud heads into 2027 without a new deal There are 17 games in the 2026 Houston Texans schedule – and hopefully, at least 3 more after those. If they win the last 3-4, Stroud will likely get paid. If not, La Canfora may seem prophetic. A lot of folks familiar with Stroud’s days at Ohio State were somewhat shocked at his early, elite-adjacent performances in the NFL. Most of those same folks are buying the current Stroud as the guy they knew all along who couldn’t get it done. On the flipside, Stroud does hold the Rose Bowl record for most passing touchdowns in a game – in a stadium that holds 100k+ people. Hard to think of a college-level game that could feel bigger than 100,000+ screaming fans within 200 yards of you at all times. Personally, I think Stroud gets it done this year and we’re all looking back saying “remember when so many people didn’t believe in him?” But, I also thought Jadeveon Clowney and J.J. Watt were going to be the best DE tandem in the NFL for the better part of a decade. In reference to the AFC South scout’s quote above, if the scout works for the Glitter Kitties or the Baby Horses, the opinion is immediately sus. If employed by the Not-The-Oilers, it’s almost impossible to take seriously. What do you think?
author: Mike Bullock

title: Value of Things: Revisiting J.D. Clowney
summary: There is probably not another sport where draft position matters more than in the NFL. In particular, number one overall picks specifically and those taken within the first handful of selections are graded very harshly. There aren’t that many Hall of Famers. There shouldn’t be. Still, first overall sections are expected to be Pro Bowl […]
full_text: There is probably not another sport where draft position matters more than in the NFL. In particular, number one overall picks specifically and those taken within the first handful of selections are graded very harshly. There aren’t that many Hall of Famers. There shouldn’t be. Still, first overall sections are expected to be Pro Bowl level players and should be in contention for the Hall of Fame. At least that is the expectation. If the Hall of Fame or the Pro Bowl is the bar then J.D. Clowney probably fails the test for a first overall pick. He officially has been to three Pro Bowls. That feels very light when you compare that with Aaron Donald who was also selected in the first round. However, he is going into his 13th season and he has been highly productive overall even if he hasn’t amassed the season to season high sack totals that were expected when he first came out of Clemson. Tackles TFL Sacks FF 2014 7 3 0.0 0 2015 40 8 4.5 1 2016 52 16 6.0 1 2017 59 21 9.5 2 2018 47 16 9.0 1 2019 31 7 3.0 4 2020 19 4 0.0 1 2021 37 11 9.0 2 2022 28 4 2.0 1 2023 43 9 9.5 2 2024 46 9 5.5 0 2025 41 12 8.5 1 Career 450 120 66.5 16 So, obviously these numbers are a mixed bag. On the one hand, it is impressive to put together a 13 year career (counting this season). Two of those seasons are a virtual wash due to injuries, so he has had a solid ten year career. Most players can’t approach that and most players from his draft are no longer in the league building their resume. The football Hall of Fame is not my personal wheelhouse like the baseball Hall of Fame, but if we look at the defensive ends and edge rushers in Canton then we will see that 100 sacks is usually the minimal litmus test to enter the door. In fact, if we look at the recent additions at the position over the last five seasons we can see what their career numbers are. Tackles TFL Sacks FF Jared Allen 648 171 136.0 31 Julius Peppers 719 175 159.5 51 Dwight Freeney 350 128 125.5 47 It’s at this point where I have to acknowledge two things. First, I absolutely love numbers. I think every reader of this feature realizes that. It eliminates a lot of the noise. When we look at these Hall of Famers we can see the clear separation between them and players like Clowney. We will also see guys like J.J. Watt fit comfortably in that group. Will Anderson certainly seems like he is on that path and Danielle Hunter is probably on that road as well. Tackles TFL Sacks FF J.J. Watt 586 195 114.5 27 Danielle Hunter 562 140 114.5 15 Will Anderson 136 46 30.0 4 Obviously, Anderson will take some projection since he has only finished three seasons. However, if we assume he continues on the pace he is on then the Texans have two Hall of Fame level defensive ends at or near the prime of their career. Watt obviously is now the number one CBS commentator, but his numbers serve as an area of reference. We say all this to say that Clowney is certainly a starting quality defensive end and has been one for a decade. The fact that he is the first end off the bench is a huge plus for the Texans in terms of depth. He probably won’t get the snaps he got in Dallas last season, but he certainly has been a productive player even if he isn’t a dominant one historically. He feels like a Mario Williams level of player in terms of being a very good performer that wasn’t consistently among the league’s best. Still, when you are a championship team, you need guys like Clowney. You need depth pieces that can come off the bench and perform to win a key game or two. It doesn’t work in this fay and age to have 11 good football players on each side and expect them to make it through the season healthy. Imagine a trade deadline in MLB and Nick Caserio got more done last week than anything happening over on Crawford street.
author: Scott Barzilla

title: Houston Texans Stock Up, Stock Down after the first week of Training Camp
summary: The Texans have completed one week of Training Camp and it’s been a learning experience to say the least. Between the rookies showcasing their skills, the injuries, and the veteran additions this first week has been as exciting as tumultuous. The offense still needs to gel, but the defense looks as formidable as ever. Let’s […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 01: British Brooks #44, Woody Marks #4 and Jawhar Jordan #26 of the Houston Texans cross the field during Houston Texans training camp at Houston Methodist Training Center on August 01, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Texans have completed one week of Training Camp and it’s been a learning experience to say the least. Between the rookies showcasing their skills, the injuries, and the veteran additions this first week has been as exciting as tumultuous. The offense still needs to gel, but the defense looks as formidable as ever. Let’s see who’s rising and falling throughout the first week of Texans Training Camp. Stock Down: Texans PR Department As much as I prefer to start on an upward trajectory, this has to be addressed. The Texans constrained their media affiliates on what they can tweet and communicate regarding depth charts, player groupings, and roster configuration. Do they not realize there are eight practices open to the public and preseason games? Fans will find out sooner or later what they’re hiding. My hunch, first-rounder Keylan Rutledge doesn’t look good and is not participating with the first or second string. The Texans PR staff has told media they are to NOT report offensive line combinations during practice. So, if you want to know who’s starting on the offensive line then you need to come to practice. There will be A LOT of shuffling early on in camp. Also, Nick Caserio says… — Will Kunkel (@WillKunkelV) July 29, 2026 This is more illogical than embarrassing… and it’s fairly embarrassing. There are eight practices open to the public, who have no media affiliation nor restriction on posting on social media. Word is going to get out one way or another as to what’s happening at camp. If anything, trying to conceal it will only make fans search harder. Stock Up: Justin Watson, WR Watson in very short time and with even less production wedged himself onto this roster as an integral part of the system. His blocking and route running are highly valued assets by Offensive Coordinator Nick Caley. Plus, the injury to Jaylin Noel opened up more reps for the veteran. Depending on Noel’s timeline, Watson has the inside track to not only make the roster but start as the WR3. Stock Down: Special Teams Jaylin Noel, Jake Hansen, and M.J. Stewart all are hurt and likely out for quite a while. They were slated to be significant contributors on special teams this season and will miss time due to various injuries. Noel is Houston’s kick and punt returner, Hansen is a tackling menace, and Stewart is phenomenal on kickoff. Noel and Stewart should be back later this season, but this phrase has been negatively impacted and we aren’t three days into practice. Stock Up: Marte Mapu and Wade Woodaz. Thanks to injury attrition, MM and WW have gone from the fringes of the roster to the backup linebackers on defense. The foot injury to Jake Hansen and quad injury to E.J. Speed immediately zapped the depth of this group. Now both Mapu and Woodaz must step up to assume the role and reps of the two injured linebackers. Stock Down: Jake Hummel The special teams linebacker was in line to earn a roster spot due to all of the injuries and youth at the position. Unfortunately, he has been nowhere to be seen since the start of training camp. Not at practice, not at the facility, nothing. In the Rosterology 2.0, Hummel was a part of the “Last Four In” to make the team. Being a no-show through the first week won’t bode well for his stock. Stock Up: Defensive depth Texans signed DL Mario Edwards, LB Sione Takitaki, and DE Jadeveon Clowney this weekend in a trio of moves to bolster the front seven. Takitaki is the third former New England Patriots LB who found their way onto Houston’s roster. These moves add more talent to the already stacked defense and integrates veterans into the room. Couldn’t be more intrigued by what Clowney brings to the defense.
author: Kenneth Levy

title: Jonathan Taylor made the Colts pay
summary: The NFL is a copycat league. When one team finds success with a certain style or play, you can bet other teams will follow suit. The same goes for players. See success, chase that same success. Bijan Robinson just became the highest paid running back in the league. Jonathan Taylor was well aware of that […]
full_text: The NFL is a copycat league. When one team finds success with a certain style or play, you can bet other teams will follow suit. The same goes for players. See success, chase that same success. Bijan Robinson just became the highest paid running back in the league. Jonathan Taylor was well aware of that new deal and made the Indianapolis Colts pay. Taylor signed a two-year extension worth $44 million worth up to $47 million and includes $39 million guaranteed, per a report from ESPN’s Adam Schefter and Ian Rapaport on Thursday monring . Taylor was informed of Robinson’s 3-year, $75 million deal during training camp earlier this week. With $51 million in guarantees, it’s a whopper. Said tongue in cheek, Taylor was looking for the Colts to pony up, which played out with an ensuing contract extension. Colts running back Jonathan Taylor, after hearing about Bijan Robinson’s extension in Atlanta, says he’s going to “tap in” with his agent “now that you guys broke the news to me.” pic.twitter.com/FTsLpM9GjI — Stephen Holder (@HolderStephen) August 4, 2026 Yes, he was joking, but then again, he was dead serious and should be. Rewind three years ago and running backs were a dime a dozen. At least that’s how the league saw them. After a zoom call, Taylor became the poster child for “running backs for better rights” and held out on the Colts. That produced a nice contract and helped reset the running back market. Robinson’s contract is a reflection of Taylor’s effort. Why shouldn’t Taylor reap the ultimate rewards himself? He was a dark horse candidate for MVP over the first ten weeks of last season. He broke huge runs, set franchise records, and carried the Colts at times. There is a lot of distance between that unfortunate offseason and the accompanying ankle injury. Time has passed but the results live on. Luckily for Taylor, he was able to cash in one more time. The Colts paid handsomely to keep Jonathan Taylor. Based on last season’s production that should be no problem. Editor’s note: This article was originally written before Taylor agreed to his contract extension and has been updated to reflect the signing.

title: Seth McGowan is making his case in the Colts’ backfield
summary: Seth McGowan arrived in Indianapolis as a seventh-round pick, which usually means expectations are low and the path to a role is narrow from the beginning. Late-round running backs do not get much handed to them, especially when the starter is Jonathan Taylor and the offense already knows where its identity begins. McGowan was never […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - AUGUST 3: Indianapolis Colts running back Seth McGowan (20) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts training camp practice on August 3, 2026 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Seth McGowan arrived in Indianapolis as a seventh-round pick, which usually means expectations are low and the path to a role is narrow from the beginning. Late-round running backs do not get much handed to them, especially when the starter is Jonathan Taylor and the offense already knows where its identity begins. McGowan was never going to walk into training camp with a job waiting for him, but running back is also one of the few positions where a late-round player can climb quickly if the style, physicality and gamestyle translate. The Colts do not have a settled backup behind Taylor, and McGowan has already started building a case that he deserves to be part of that conversation. He led Kentucky with 725 rushing yards and 12 touchdowns last season, and the early camp buzz has centered on the way he runs: decisive, physical and willing to finish through contact. Shane Steichen summed up the appeal pretty clearly, saying McGowan is “not scared of contact,” which is exactly the kind of trait coaches want to see from a rookie back trying to earn trust. McGowan’s profile is not hard to understand. He is a bigger back who can get downhill and run behind his pads, but he is not just a short-yardage grinder. There is enough burst to win outside when the lane is there, which matters because the Colts do not need a backup who only gives them predictable carries between the tackles. They need someone who can keep the offense functional when Taylor is off the field, whether that means hammering inside runs, pressing the edge or making enough happen on his own when the blocking is not perfect. Rookie RB, Seth McGowan with a nice outside run 💨 pic.twitter.com/ViaWIsC8uw — Logan Hancock (@ProFanLogan) August 4, 2026 That is where the battle with DJ Giddens becomes important. Giddens, a 2025 fifth-round pick, has a similar general profile and came into the league with a tad more draft investment behind him, but he did very little last season and has not done enough to lock down the RB2 job. If McGowan looks more decisive, more physical or more explosive through camp and the preseason, the fact that he was picked in the seventh round will not hold him back. Jonathan Taylor’s comments about McGowan are also telling. Taylor reportedly compared him to David Montgomery, which does not mean McGowan is about to become Montgomery or that the Colts have already found a future starter. It does, however, give a pretty clear idea of what stands out. Montgomery has built a strong NFL career by being tough, decisive and difficult to bring down cleanly. He is not the flashiest back in the league, but he runs with conviction, finishes plays and consistently gets more than what is blocked. If Taylor sees even some of that in McGowan, it explains why the rookie is already getting attention. The timing matters too. Taylor is still the engine of the Colts’ offense, but he is entering the final year of his contract and has dealt with injuries in past seasons. The team has also talked about finding ways to take some of the workload off him, which only works if another running back earns real trust. The backup job is not just a roster footnote this year. It could mean six to eight touches a game, more work if Taylor misses time, and a much larger role next season if the Colts and Taylor do not work out another deal. That does not mean McGowan should be treated like the obvious future at running back before he has played an NFL game. He still has to prove the parts of the position that decide whether young backs actually get on the field, especially pass protection, ball security, consistency and special teams value. Running hard is a great starting point, but coaches need to know a rookie will not get the quarterback hit, catch a pass if needed or put the ball on the ground. The Colts need a real backup behind Taylor, Giddens has not separated himself, and McGowan has the kind of physical style that can show up quickly once the pads come on. He does not need to become the future starter right now. He just needs to prove he is too useful to ignore, and on a roster without a clear No. 2 back, that may be enough to make him one of the more interesting young players in Colts camp.

title: Chiefs training camp notebook Day 8: The defense has ‘long way to go’
summary: The eighth practice of Kansas City Chiefs training camp was a mild one in comparison to the other seven. After three consecutive days in full pads, the team was mandated to have a lightened practice on Thursday ahead of donning the pads again Friday and Saturday. By all accounts, most of the work done on […]
full_text: Jul 29, 2026; St. Joseph, MO, USA; Kansas City Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo walks down the hill to the fields prior to training camp at Missouri Western State University. Mandatory Credit: Denny Medley-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The eighth practice of Kansas City Chiefs training camp was a mild one in comparison to the other seven. After three consecutive days in full pads, the team was mandated to have a lightened practice on Thursday ahead of donning the pads again Friday and Saturday. By all accounts, most of the work done on the field was basically a sped-up walkthrough, working on timing and the details of plays without full-speed contact to disrupt things. After practice, defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo was able to share a state of the defense after a week of camp. Spags needs to see ‘a lot’ from Mansoor Delane before Week 1 Still wearing a yellow, non-contact jersey, rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane has been unable to show Spagnuolo the full extent of his abilities so far. “We’re trying to be a little cautious with the shoulder, the shoulder blade,” Spagnuolo told reporters. “He was out there today because we only had shells on so he could protect himself. The other three days, with the shoulder pads, it was just really being safe, protecting him from himself because we don’t want to set him back.” “He did a good job,” Spaguolo noted. “You saw him in and out of huddles, getting everything mentally, trying to keep the conditioning up. We’ll see where we are tomorrow, because we put the pads back on.” The defensive coach was asked what he needs to see from Delane before the team takes the field against the Denver Broncos in Week 1. “A lot,” Spagnuolo said. “We just haven’t had the work; you go through OTAs, and it’s just helmets. The thing he’s missing right now is the continuity with a bunch of guys that are new to him; everybody’s new, so we’re going to have to fight through that; before you know, we’re going to be lining up against Denver. Hopefully we can get him back quicker than we thought.” Peter Woods has ‘a ways to go’ When asked about rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods, Spagnuolo excitedly tried to describe the good things he has put on display at camp. “That’s the way they’re supposed to look, right?” Spagnuolo asked the media. “I think he has a ways to go,” he continued. “Some of these younger guys aren’t really used to the way we do things, and that’s for all the rookies. Pete’s right in there with that crew, but when he does get his feet right, he does keep his pad level low; he’s a pretty good football player. It’s our job to get him to do that every down, and he’s a willing guy. I like him; he’s a smart, good football player.” Regardless of how much Woods still has to pick up as an NFL player, Spagnuolo admits that the interior positions may be better set up for a young, learning player to make an impact. “It’s pretty well defined as what an inside guy does as a three-technique or an A-gap tackle,” Spaguolo acknowledged. “We’ve got a few multiple things we’re looking at, so I think Pete’s learning some things that maybe he didn’t do before, and we’d like to find out what he can do. I believe in having as many versatile players as we can, so he’ll be thrown in that same category.” Spags needs to see more physicality and violence When prompted to summarize his unit’s performance throughout camp, a negative day in “goal-line” work stood out in Spagnuolo’s head. It’s clear that Kansas City’s defensive coordinator needs to see more of his defense in live action. “If I’m assessing the three days in pads, I would say we have a long way to go with our physicality and our violent play,” Spagnuolo said. “Yet, you’re going against your own team, so you have to play that game, but hopefully we can get enough of those snaps in the preseason games to see where we are.” When zoning in on the defensive backfield, Spags talked through the lack of vocal leadership compared to previous seasons. He mentioned the loud communication of former Chiefs safety Bryan Cook while also pointing to cornerback Trent McDuffie stirring the pot. “It’s going to take a little while before this group gets comfortable together,” Spagnuolo admitted. “Hopefully sooner rather than later… I think Alohi will be that kind of guy; he’s just still learning the defense, too.” Ending on a positive note: Felix Anudike-Uzomah One day after head coach Andy Reid emphasized improvement in the get-off of defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah, Spagnuolo doubled down on a growing narrative from the week of practices: Anudike-Uzomah is playing well. “I think he’s had a really good camp,” Spagnuolo said. “He’s fought these injuries all the way through; even when he was playing, I think he was hampered by it… When I’ve had my brief conversations, it feels like it’s the healthiest he has been.” “He has been in the system now for the fourth year, so he should know it,” Spagnuolo pointed out. “I think he has had some pretty effective, productive plays, and I’m hoping that continues… Ashton [Gillotte], we need him out there too, but the blessing in disguise for Felix is he gets more reps, so hopefully it keeps being positive.” The Chiefs will be back on the practice field in pads on Friday morning, starting at 9:15 a.m.

title: In Cyrus Allen, Chiefs reportedly see ‘similarities’ to Stefon Diggs
summary: We are over a week into Kansas City Chiefs training camp, which has given the national media time to make stops in St. Joe to take in practice. Albert Breer, senior NFL reporter for Sports Illustrated, visited practices this week and shared insight in an article from earlier this week, emptying out his notebook with […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Cyrus Allen #13 runs with the ball during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We are over a week into Kansas City Chiefs training camp, which has given the national media time to make stops in St. Joe to take in practice. Albert Breer, senior NFL reporter for Sports Illustrated , visited practices this week and shared insight in an article from earlier this week , emptying out his notebook with plenty about the team heading into the 2026 season. One particular note about rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen, currently recovering from a bone bruise on his shin, stood out: The bigger questions lingering are elsewhere in the skill group, particularly at receiver. Rashee Rice, coming off injury, needs to be more dependable—he’s still working his way back. Third-year man Xavier Worthy has had a really solid camp, and looks ready to take a step. And rookie Cyrus Allen, a fifth-rounder out of Cincinnati, might’ve been the best receiver in camp before bruising his shin; he’s expected back soon. The Chiefs see some similarities to Stefon Diggs in physical profile and play style in Allen, and he’s very much part of the offensive plan. The stylistic comparison to veteran free agent Stefon Diggs is interesting, but it’s also noteworthy to me that Diggs is a former fifth-round pick (146th overall), just like Allen (176th overall). With the talent Allen has flashed so far in camp, is it possible the Chiefs struck gold late in the draft with a Pro Bowl-level wideout? Diggs didn’t reach 1,000 single-season receiving yards until his fourth year in the NFL, but in the prime of his career, he ripped off four consecutive Pro Bowl seasons, including a 2020 campaign that featured him as the NFL leader in receptions (127) and receiving yards (1,535). If the excitement for Allen wasn’t already boiling over, it’s overwhelming to consider Allen as the breakout Day 3 offensive playmaker of this year’s draft. Whether it was Diggs in 2015 or Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua a few years ago, these underrated pass catchers come around every once in a while, and signs are pointing to Allen being next in line.

title: Emari Demarcado is embracing his ‘niche in the league’ with the Chiefs
summary: If you come into the league as an undrafted free agent who is hoping to stick, you have to learn how to do the little things right and make yourself valuable. And aside from one glaring mistake he made against the Tennessee Titans in Week 5 of last season, one of the Kansas City Chiefs‘ […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Emari Demercado #25 smiles as he walks to the field before practice during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images If you come into the league as an undrafted free agent who is hoping to stick, you have to learn how to do the little things right and make yourself valuable. And aside from one glaring mistake he made against the Tennessee Titans in Week 5 of last season, one of the Kansas City Chiefs ‘ newest additions to the running back room has done just that. Genuinely curious, why do players do this? Emari Demarcado must have seen Adonai Mitchell do this JUST LAST WEEK and yet…. pic.twitter.com/KiBkQwoeSz — James D Koh (@JamesDKoh) October 5, 2025 If you haven’t seen Demarcado’s infamous highlight, this is the mistake I’m referring to. But even when it happened, Demarcado didn’t make any excuses for himself. “I can’t expect myself to be perfect,” Demercado said. “No one is. I had to let (the incident) go. That’s not who I am. Everybody messes up. Unfortunately, mine was that. “I’ve seen the replay. Bonehead play. You look at it, you shake your head. … I definitely thought I was in. But emotions, I let them get the best of me.” Instead, in the following weeks, he started trying to make a new name for himself. Fans wanted Demercado to be released, lashing out in anger over social media. But the one-time undrafted rookie was on the roster for a reason. The Cardinals needed him. And that was emphasized again Monday in the win over the Cowboys, when Demercado rushed for a team-best 79 yards on only 14 carries and provided QB Jacoby Brissett with a number of key blocks that helped make the passing game go. “I put who I am back on tape,” the understated Demercado said. “You make one mistake and the whole world kind of flames you for it. (Monday was) to set the record straight.” It was Demarcado’s pass blocking that caught the eye of the media covering the Arizona Cardinals , and it’s what’s caught the eye of Kansas City’s coaching staff as well. “I like the pass protection,” Chiefs head coach Andy Reid described Demarcado after practice on Wednesday. “He’s not going to bounce anything; he sees it, he lowers it, and he hits it in the run game; I think that’s important. Pass routes are pretty good. He’s played; he has experience; it’s just pushing yourself through this workload, and I like what I’ve seen the last couple of days.” For everyone wondering why the Cardinals like Emari Demercado so much: pic.twitter.com/8srL6gthUQ — Theo Mackie (@theo_mackie) October 29, 2024 Pass protection isn’t something that came naturally to Demarcado, or as he once put it to a reporter while he was in Arizona: “I sucked at it in college.” But he worked at it, and now, as he battles to carve out a role for himself as the third-down back on Kansas City’s offense, it’s once again begun to pay dividends for Demarcado. “I take a lot of pride [in pass protection],” Demarcado told the media after practice on Wednesday. “I think that’s just where I found my niche in the league.” Especially when you consider who he is tasked with protecting this time around. And that’s not a knock on Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett, but not all signal callers are created the same. Some players are more valuable to their team than others, and you’ll be hard-pressed to find a player more important to the fortunes of their franchise than quarterback Patrick Mahomes. It’s not something Demarcado takes lightly. “To stay on top of that and protect somebody like Pat, that’s a big deal,” Demarcado emphasized. “So I take a lot of pride in that.” Some lessons can only be taught through taking reps and learning from your experiences. And it’s this experience that Demarcado has gained through his successes and failures that so far is giving him a hand up in the battle to be the third-down back, against younger and less experienced players like rookie Emmett Johnson, who, as Andy Reid noted on Wednesday, is “learning as he goes…” “He’s pushing himself,” continued Reid, speaking about Johnson. “You saw a couple of these where he has to drop that pad level down. You go in high at this level, you’re going to get rearranged, and you don’t want that to happen.” At the end of the day, I don’t care if it’s Demarcado, Johnson, or Gandalf standing in the backfield shouting, “You shall not pass!” to oncoming defensive tackles and Balrogs. As long as Patrick Mahomes stays upright, that’s all I care about. And right now, it seems Demarcado has the inside track to be that guy.

title: Chiefs News: Chiefs drop ‘GEHA’ from Arrowhead Stadium name
summary: The latest The home of the Kansas City Chiefs is once again Arrowhead Stadium. Not GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium. No, just Arrowhead Stadium. It has been that way since 1972, so the team “shedding” the sponsorship is not only welcome, but a nice way to pay tribute to a legendary stadium before the team […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - AUGUST 22: Kansas City Chiefs flag team after a score against the Chicago Bears on August 22nd, 2025 at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri (Photo by William Purnell/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The latest The home of the Kansas City Chiefs is once again Arrowhead Stadium. Not GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium. No, just Arrowhead Stadium. It has been that way since 1972, so the team “shedding” the sponsorship is not only welcome, but a nice way to pay tribute to a legendary stadium before the team moves across the state line in 2031. Kansas City Chiefs drop GEHA Field from stadium, return to simply Arrowhead Stadium | Associated Press The Chiefs and GEHA signed a naming rights deal in 2021 that resulted in the name change. But it never stuck among fans, and even players and coaches often forgot to use the official moniker, instead using the name it was christened with upon opening in 1972. In fact, Arrowhead Stadium has become such a well-known brand that just about everybody in Kansas City and beyond continued to refer to it that way during the recent World Cup, when FIFA renamed it “Kansas City Stadium” for the six matches played there. Eight observations from Day 7 of Chiefs camp: Kahlil Benson takes control at RT | The Kansas City Star In 11-on-11 near the 25-yard line, Mahomes drew the defense in to set up a screen for Kenneth Walker, who likely would have taken it for a touchdown in a game setting. Closer to the goal line, Mahomes nearly had a touchdown pass to Travis Kelce, but Kelce couldn’t keep his feet in bounds from my vantage point. From the 10-yard line, wide receiver Tyquan Thornton high-pointed a pass from Mahomes along the left sideline and, despite being elevated, found a way to toe-tap in bounds to complete the reception. A few plays later, the quarterback threw a quick pass to tight end Noah Gray, who scored the first of four touchdowns during team periods on the day. As the Chiefs experiment with heavier looks, especially in scoring areas, Gray remains a target to watch. Jake Briningstool and 4 more Kansas City Chiefs players with stock on the rise after first week of training camp practices | A to Z Sports S Xavier Nwankpa Dave Toub put Nwankpa on everyone’s radar back in June. Now, Nwankpa is putting himself squarely on the radar through his play during practice. He’s primarily worked with the second-team defense at safety, along with special teams. On defense, he’s flashed numerous times. His interception and return against Justin Fields on the first day of pads stood out most. Nick Jacobs’ Chiefs Camp Notebook: It’s Noah Gray Day in St. Joseph | KSHB Quarterback Patrick Mahomes and tight end Noah Gray connected on multiple touchdown throws during red zone work. The first touchdown Mahomes was able to bullet between two defenders. The second one, Gray was able to keep the defender at bay and catch the far-shoulder throw. Rookie quarterback Garrett Nussmeier made an impressive throw on the run and placed it in a spot where only wide receiver Omari Evans could reach for a sliding touchdown. Kansas City Chiefs reveal limited-edition Red Thursday flag for 2026 | KMBC Similar to last year, the 13th edition of the flag displays head coach Andy Reid’s iconic phrase, “How ‘Bout Those Chiefs,” this time on a red background with white and gold lettering. Flags are available for presale here starting at 10 a.m. Thursday, Aug. 6. Fans can snag a flag for a $10 donation, with proceeds going toward the Ronald McDonald House Kansas City. Around the NFL Sources: WR Stefon Diggs set to sign with Commanders | ESPN Diggs strengthens a receiver group whose depth had improved from 2025 but was still facing questions at the top, aside from McLaurin. Diggs, who was born in suburban Washington and played collegiately at Maryland, had made his desire to play for the Commanders known. Diggs attended Maryland’s first fall practice Wednesday and the university shared a video message on Instagram from the former Terrapins wide receiver. “Shout out to my Terps and go Commanders,” he said in the video. “Let’s go!” Sean McVay on Aaron Donald’s Rams tryout: ‘I think he can make the team’ | The Athletic Labeling the workout at the Rams’ facility as a “tryout” was a formality to comply with league rules and processes, head coach Sean McVay later said in an interview with NFL Daily, which is why it appeared on the league’s official transaction wire. “Best tryout that we’ve ever had,” a grinning McVay said. “I think he can make the team.” D.J. Jones says Broncos can break ‘84 Bears’ sack record: ‘We’re about to eat again’ | NFL.com “We can break it. We can break the record,” the veteran defensive tackle said Wednesday when asked about the Broncos’ sack goals in 2026. “What is that, 72? We can break it.” Those 72 sacks were compiled by the 1984 Bears, one of the best defenses in the history of the game. And Chicago set that mark in just 16 games, as compared to the 17 that the current Broncos have to work with. The ’25 Broncos’ 68 quarterback takedowns are tied for fifth-most all time behind the ’84 Bears, ’89 Vikings (71), ’22 Eagles (70) and ’87 Bears (70). Jones isn’t the only Denver defender who’s been confident this offseason about snapping Chicago’s record. Pass rush mate Zach Allen said in early July that the Broncos “fully expect to break it” in 2026. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Khyiris Tonga: ‘Peter Woods is a little pitbull’ “P-Woods, he’s a little pitbull,” defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga said after Tuesday’s practice. “He’s nasty. He’s got something to him, and he’s got a chip on his shoulder. [He’s] eager to learn — just a sponge. Just taking everything in and just learning and growing, it’s cool to see that. Really, all the rookies too. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs are coming off their worst season in over a decade. 2025 was not only the first losing season of the Patrick Mahomes era, but it was also the first losing season for head coach Andy Reid since joining the organization in 2013. Finishing 6-11, the Chiefs lost eight of their final nine games in 2025, including losses to division rivals the Denver Broncos , Las Vegas Raiders , and Los Angeles Chargers . There were a lot of factors that played into the Chiefs’ disappointing 2025 campaign. Like the fact that the Chiefs’ pass rush was exclusively found on a milk carton, or the absence of any hint of explosiveness at the running back position. Kansas City’s season was already in the trash heap by the time Mahomes tore his ACL in the Week 15 loss to the Chargers. Still, there is no doubt that Mahomes’ injury is when things went from bad to a dumpster fire. For a team that appeared in three straight Super Bowls from 2022-2024 (winning two of them), 2025’s fall from grace was a stark reminder that in today’s NFL, the fate of a franchise is constantly ebbing and flowing. As hard as the climb to the top is, the fall from grace is twice as sudden and bumpy on the way down. If the Chiefs want to climb out of the AFC West cellar and improve on last season’s third-place finish, they need to be more balanced on offense and find a way to get to the opposing quarterback. Kansas City seems to think they’ve figured out the solution to these problems. The Chiefs signed star running back Kenneth Walker in free agency this offseason, and on the defensive side of the ball, Kansas City invested heavily in the pass rush by selecting defensive lineman Peter Woods and edge rusher R Mason Thomas within the top 100 picks of the draft. In addition, the Chiefs retooled their coaching staff on offense, bringing offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy back into the fold, as well as hiring new running backs coach Demarco Murray and wide receivers coach Chad O’Shea. The big question is, have the Chiefs done enough to contend for a Super Bowl in 2026? FanDuel Sportsbook seems to think so. The Over/Under win total for the Chiefs is set at 10.5 this season, and has given Kansas City the fifth-best odds in the NFL to make the playoffs at -184. title: Chiefs training camp notebook Day 7: Josh Simmons is up a weight class
summary: On Wednesday, the Kansas City Chiefs had a weather-impacted practice for the second time in seven practices at training camp in St. Joe. This time, the team moved indoors for a good portion of practice, then came back out and finished on the wet grass fields to cap off the longest start-to-finish practice of camp. […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Josh Simmons #71 walks to the field before practice during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images On Wednesday, the Kansas City Chiefs had a weather-impacted practice for the second time in seven practices at training camp in St. Joe. This time, the team moved indoors for a good portion of practice, then came back out and finished on the wet grass fields to cap off the longest start-to-finish practice of camp. In this post-practice interview with CBS Sports’ Evan Washburn, head coach Andy Reid praised the players for staying focused through “sudden change.” It seemed like the old ball coach enjoyed putting his team through a unique circumstance, one that was rare, according to defensive tackle Chris Jones in a separate interview with Washburn . “It started lightning earlier; we went inside. The first time ever, in 11 years, we came back to the field,” Jones told Washburn. “It was a really, really good practice… get out here so the fans can see us and give us a little energy on defense.” Due to the rain, there were limited in-person observations from the Arrowhead Pride crew today. Check out the notes that were taken down in The Feed this morning . Reid broke down the list of injured players after practice, but he also provided notes on a few different players . One of the most significant was about second-year left tackle Josh Simmons. Andy Reid approves of Josh Simmons going up a weight class Reid was asked about Simmons’ weight in his press conference, a point of discussion among many in Chiefs Kingdom this offseason when he debuted a stronger, bigger physique during OTAs. “He put on weight in the offseason; he’s been able to maintain it,” Reid told the media. “I think it’ll help him, not that he couldn’t do it at the other weight, but this gives him a little bit more lead in his pants, and that pays off over time during the season.” In his own post-practice press conference on Wednesday, Simmons confirmed he is playing at a weight the team is satisfied with. “It’s definitely where it needs to be,” Simmons said about his weight. Simmons is paired up with third-year left guard Kingsley Suamataia on one side of the line. The two are building their chemistry; Reid has taken note. “You can see them communicating,” Reid noted. “Kingsley does a nice job with that, making sure Josh gets all the calls and everything. The more they play together, the better it’ll be; they’re both very gifted athletically, it’s just a matter of technique, fundamentals and all that stuff. They work like crazy on it.” “I understand how he goes about blocks now,” Simmons said of Suamataia. “What he’s seeing when he’s coming to the line. If I can understand and kind of have that telepathy with him, I think that we can play a lot faster.” On the other side of the offensive line, rookie right tackle Kahlil Benson seems to be settling in as a potential long-term starter alongside Simmons and Suamataia. Before we all get too far ahead of ourselves, Simmons has given Benson advice on how to proceed from a strong initial impression. “I think Kahlil’s doing a great job; he’s a very physical player,” Simmons shared. “I think he should just add onto that; I don’t think you can really teach effort. I mean, that’s what he’s giving out there, so that’s really all I’m telling him right now.” R Mason Thomas is testing Simmons, Chiefs’ offensive line “Extremely explosive,” Simmons described rookie edge rusher R Mason Thomas. “You almost have to be offsides to stay in front of him. I think he’ll definitely keep me and any tackle on their toes to make sure we’re on the snap count, for sure.” Get ready for Simmons leading the way on screen passes “Extremely scary,” Simmons said about running back Kenneth Walker when asked about the screen game. “We kind of know what [Walker] does and what he’s capable of doing. As long as we can just target and get to our assignments, we know he’s going to take us home. One-hundred percent.” Other notes from Andy Reid Fourth-year defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah is looking for a career resurgence in 2026. One aspect of his game that lacked early in his career was speed off the ball. Reid has noted improvement in that area. “With Gillotte down, he’s getting a few more reps in there, doing a nice job,” Reid said. “You can tell that his explosion off the ball is better… way different at getting off the ball. If there’s one thing that jumps out at me, it’s that.” It was a strong day for the tight ends at training camp Wednesday. Noah Gray was the star of practice, but second-year tight end Jake Briningstool has finally been able to showcase his skills to Reid and the coaching staff after missing nearly all of last offseason with a hamstring injury. “It’s great that he’s back-to-back in these practices here, then you get a chance to see what he’s all about,” Reid said of the former Clemson tight end. “He’s a good receiver, and he’s stuck his nose in there, and he’s blocking. My hat goes off to him; he just has to keep stacking them right now.” Without wide receivers Xavier Worthy and rookie Cyrus Allen in the mix for practice Tuesday and Wednesday, two lesser-known names have stepped up: Andrew Armstrong and Jimmy Holiday. “I like what Armstrong’s doing,” Reid pointed out. “He’s a big kid, strong, looks like the quarterbacks trust him… they trust him on his route running. He’s got good speed for a big kid and good transition; he’s not stiff coming out of breaks.” “Jimmy’s the other one,” Reid continued. “He’s really shown the last few days here, and that’s important for his job here.”

title: Andy Reid gives injury update after Wednesday’s Chiefs camp practice
summary: The seventh full-team practice of Kansas City Chiefs training camp took place on a rainy morning in St. Joe. After a brief warm-up, the team went inside to begin practice, but came back out for roughly an hour to finish practice on the grass fields at Missouri Western State University. After its conclusion, head coach […]
full_text: ST JOSEPH, MISSOURI - JULY 30: Head coach Andy Reid participates during Kansas City Chiefs training camp at Missouri Western State University on July 30, 2026 in St Joseph, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The seventh full-team practice of Kansas City Chiefs training camp took place on a rainy morning in St. Joe. After a brief warm-up, the team went inside to begin practice, but came back out for roughly an hour to finish practice on the grass fields at Missouri Western State University. After its conclusion, head coach Andy Reid provided an injury update that was the longest it has been all of camp. He began by sharing that rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen, who has not practiced since sustaining a bone bruise during Monday’s practice, is “making improvement.” He added that defensive end Ashton Gillotte, out of practice with a hamstring strain since last Friday, is “making progress.” The same note was made of wide receiver Xavier Worthy, who missed a second practice due to a shoulder injury. Cornerback Kristian Fulton missed his second consecutive practice on Wednesday with a hip-flexor strain, according to Reid. During Wednesday’s practice, the linebacker position suffered two injuries that took players in the starting mix off the field. Chiefs LB Drue Tranquill has made an appearance in the training tent. pic.twitter.com/y9eFJldWDV — Matt Derrick (@mattderrick) August 5, 2026 Second-year linebacker Jeffrey Bassa suffered a groin strain, and veteran linebacker Drue Tranquill was seen off to the side of practice working through an ailment. “We’ll just see where that goes,” Reid said of Bassa. “Tranquill just had a little back spasm, so we backed off him there,” Reid added. In the place of Tranquill and Bassa was veteran linebacker Jack Cochrane, who is entering his fifth season with the Chiefs. He has earned a strong reputation among the coaching staff during that time. “Jack knows all the positions; he knows everything,” Reid said. “He’s a good special teams player on top of that. You feel comfortable, as a coach, putting him in any of those spots, and he knows that part of it. You need a couple guys like that out there.” In a positive trend at the receiver position, Rashee Rice took a step forward in his journey to 100% by participating in full-team, 11-on-11 periods for the first time this camp. “He got a lot of good reps today, which is important,” Reid said of Rice. “We just have to ease him back in and keep working, and we know he’s a good football player. You could see it actually got better as practice went on.” After a third consecutive day in pads at training camp, a lighter practice is anticipated for Thursday, starting at 9:15 a.m.
