title: Roster news: NY Giants place DT Roy Robertson-Harris on injured reserve
summary: The New York Giants made four roster moves prior to practice on Wednesday, 8/5. The Giants announced that they’ve placed defensive tackle Roy Robertson-Harris on the injured reserve, as well as waiving wide receiver Beaux Collins with an injury designation. Those two moves create a pair of needed roster openings after the team signed cornerbacks […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants defensive tackle Roy Robertson-Harris celebrates with pass rusher Brian Burns after sacking Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Geno Smith | Getty Images The New York Giants made four roster moves prior to practice on Wednesday, 8/5. The Giants announced that they’ve placed defensive tackle Roy Robertson-Harris on the injured reserve, as well as waiving wide receiver Beaux Collins with an injury designation. Those two moves create a pair of needed roster openings after the team signed cornerbacks David Long and DJ James . Long was originally drafted by the Los Angeles Rams out of Michigan in the 3rd round of the 2019 NFL Draft. He has adequate size and speed, at 5-foot-11, 196 pounds, with a 4.45-second 40 at the 2019 Combine, though he does have elite quickness, agility, and explosiveness. Long’s 3-cone drill (6.45 seconds) and short shuttle (3.97 seconds) were by far the best among corners at the 2019 Combine. Long bounced around the NFL after his first four seasons with the Rams, spending time with the Las Vegas Raiders, Green Bay Packers, Carolina Panthers (twice), and Indianapolis Colts. This is, in fact, Long’s second stint with the Giants, after he spent the 2024 off-season with the Giants before being waived in that year’s final roster cuts. DJ James was originally drafted out of Auburn in the 6th round of the 2024 draft by the Seattle Seahawks. James started his collegiate career at Oregon before transferring to Auburn and was a highly regarded corner at both schools. He’s undersized at 5-foot-11, 175 pounds, but has very good agility and short-area quickness, and he showed a good feel for both man and zone coverage in college. James was waived in the Seahawks’ final roster cuts and signed with the New England Patriots’ practice squad in 2024, which is where he also spent 2025. The Giants had previously hoped that DT Roy Robertson-Harris could return late in the season after suffering a torn Achilles early in the off-season. However, that hope has been put to rest and the Giants officially ended his season by placing him on the injured reserve prior to the start of the season. Robertson-Harris was a starter for the Giants in 2025 and was in line to compete for a starting job this year. WR Beaux Collins was competing for a spot as a reserve wide receiver and special teams player. He signed with the Giants as an undrafted free agent out of Notre Dame following the 2025 NFL Draft, and was the only undrafted player to make the team last year. Collins struggled with route running last year, but also became a favorite among fans after he generated highlight reel plays in camp and preseason games.

title: NY Giants’ safety Tyler Nubin hopes ‘opportunistic’ scheme unlocks ball skills
summary: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — New York Giants safety Tyler Nubin was a ballhawk while playing collegiately for Minnesota, with 13 interceptions, 11 passes defensed, and three forced fumbles in 55 games. That kind of production is why the Giants, who had seen safeties Julian Love and Xavier McKinney leave in free agency the previous […]
full_text: Tyler Nubin | Getty Images WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — New York Giants safety Tyler Nubin was a ballhawk while playing collegiately for Minnesota, with 13 interceptions, 11 passes defensed, and three forced fumbles in 55 games. That kind of production is why the Giants, who had seen safeties Julian Love and Xavier McKinney leave in free agency the previous couple of offseasons, selected Nubin 47th in the 2024 NFL Draft. The production has not translated. In 26 games over two seasons, Nubin has just three passes defensed, one fumble recovery, and no interceptions. Nubin said Tuesday that he is hoping defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson’s scheme, similar to what he was asked to do at Minnesota, will lead to better production. #NYGiants safety Tyler Nubin discusses his offseason weight loss. — Ed Valentine (@edvalentine.bsky.social) 2026-08-05T16:25:11.654Z “It’s (Wilson’s scheme) great, man. It gives you a lot of opportunity to make plays. You got your eyes on the quarterback, and I think that’s something that I do very well, so something I’m really comfortable with, something I did a lot in college, so it’s going to be good,” Nubin said on Tuesday. “I think Dennard always has opportunistic defenses, looking back where he’s been, because they attack, and they make the offense think, gets them on their heels a little bit, whether that’s with the disguises or how we’re playing things, certain concepts. We can have our eyes on the quarterback and really go attack the football, so yeah, I think it’s definitely going to give me a really good opportunity for sure.” Wilson’s coverage scheme is zone-based, using a lot of two-high safeties, quarters coverage, and cornerbacks aggressively pressing wide receivers at the line of scrimmage. Nubin was asked to explain how zone-based coverage, often thought of as softer than man-to-man coverage, can be considered an attacking style. “Because it’s aggressive, man, especially when you have corners who can cover, especially when you have linebackers like we have. (Inside linebacker) Tremaine (Edmunds) and (inside linebacker) Arvell (Reese), who’s going to make that ball sail over the top.” Nubin said. “It allows you to be more aggressive on keying into the quarterback and where he’s going and jumping routes, whether that’s across the middle, whether that’s deep post routes, going to the post. So, it just allows you to go attack the football.” Nubin, whose athleticism has been pointed to by some as a possible reason for some of his struggles with play-making and tackling, lost eight pounds this offseason. He is back to his rookie playing weight of 205 pounds. “Just speed, man,” Nubin said when asked why he shed the weight. “I think my rookie year I played at like 205. Last year I was at like 213, 214. And right now, I’m like 205, 206, around there. So, I just wanted more for speed. I feel like I’m the strongest I’ve ever been, best shape I’ve ever been. So, I like this weight. I think I’m moving well.” Nubin has yet to make any big plays on the ball during camp. He and the Giants, though, are hopeful those will come. “I think he’s doing a good job. I do like the way he’s practicing. He’s a very determined, very serious-minded guy. He really wants to do well,” said head coach John Harbaugh. “He thinks about everything. He asks all the right questions. Sometimes you want to just say, “Hey, it’s not that complicated.” But you appreciate that about a player like that. So, I expect him to get back to where he was in college with the ball production. That would be great. “I’d love to see him get his hands on a lot of footballs.”

title: Geno Smith doesn’t get much love in Mike Sando’s quarterback rankings
summary: Every year Mike Sando of The Athletic polls NFL executives and coaches about the league’s quarterbacks. The votes rank the relevant quarterbacks in the NFL and place them into tiers. It probably doesn’t come as a major surprise, but coming off a rough 2025 season Geno Smith did not rate highly. Smith was in Tier […]
full_text: FLORHAM PARK, NEW JERSEY - JULY 29: Geno Smith #7 of the New York Jets throws during training camp at Atlantic Health Jets Training Center on July 29, 2026 in Florham Park, New Jersey. (Photo by Adam Hunger/Getty Images) | Getty Images Every year Mike Sando of The Athletic polls NFL executives and coaches about the league’s quarterbacks. The votes rank the relevant quarterbacks in the NFL and place them into tiers . It probably doesn’t come as a major surprise, but coming off a rough 2025 season Geno Smith did not rate highly. Smith was in Tier 4, which is defined as: Veteran who ideally would not be a full-season starter Unproven player; not enough information to classify Smith came in at 30th of the 35 passers who were part of the ranking. Smith suffered the largest year-over-year decline of any quarterback, falling from a career-best 2.90 average to 3.70. His 11-spot drop in the rankings tied Stroud’s for the largest. “He looked terrible on the film we saw,” a defensive coordinator said. The Raiders did Smith no favors. “He got sacked 10 times in a game (against Cleveland),” a defensive coach said. “Once you get hit and keep getting hit and hit and hit, how good are you going to be? They had no identity on offense. Geno got a bad rap. He was getting murdered out there.” Seven current GMs placed Smith in Tier 4. The eighth had him in Tier 5. Coaches liked Smith more than execs did. “It’s hard to tell because last year wasn’t fair, and before that he was a 3,” an offensive coach said. “I’m going to give him the benefit of the doubt and say he’s a 3 till proven otherwise.” The five quarterbacks to rank lower than Geno were Deshaun Watson, Michael Penix, Jr. Jacoby Brissett, JJ McCarthy, and Shedeur Sanders. Smith has his work cut out for him to revitalize his career. A happy Jets season will require the type of performance that lands him much higher on the 2027 quarterback ranking.

If you scroll down to the last link in today’s Flight Connections you come to an article titled “Brandon Stephens is quickly giving Jets fans a reason to forget about Sauce Gardner.” Ummm … what?! Brandon Stephens is a 28 year old journeyman who probably shouldn’t be starting in the NFL. For his career Stephens has allowed a 105+ passer rating in coverage. No quarterback in the history of the NFL has a 105+ career passer rating. Which means throwing at Stephens essentially turns the average NFL quarterback into the best quarterback of all time. Last year Stephens allowed an ungodly 134+ passer rating, the worst of his NFL career, so it’s not like he’s on the upswing in his career. Sauce Gardner is a two time All Pro. He has allowed a passer rating of 76.7 for his career. Last season the 32nd ranked NFL passer was Joe Flacco, with a 79.2 passer rating. Throwing at Gardner essentially turns the average NFL starting quarterback into worse than the worst starting quarterback in the NFL. So here’s what we have. Throw at Stephens, get results better than the best QB in NFL history. Throw at Sauce, get results worse than the worst starting quarterback in the NFL. But sure, a few decent Stephens practices in August no doubt will make Jets fans forget about their former two time All Pro cornerback. Makes perfect sense when you really think about it. The irony here is that even the author of that article doesn’t believe his own headline. Read past the headline and you see he doesn’t even try to make the case his headline implies. He knows better than that. He just wanted to put up a clickbait headline full of absurd hype, because clicks are apparently more important than not misleading your audience. Sigh. title: Ex-Jets Progress Report: Part 2 (AFC)
summary: With training camp underway, it’s a good time to keep track of where any former Jets are currently playing, so we can start to access how likely they are to have successful seasons elsewhere, or to lose their jobs and potentially become available for a reunion with the Jets. We are covering this over two […]
full_text: Browns linebacker Quincy Williams celebrates after a play during a practice, June 2, 2026, in Berea. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co With training camp underway, it’s a good time to keep track of where any former Jets are currently playing, so we can start to access how likely they are to have successful seasons elsewhere, or to lose their jobs and potentially become available for a reunion with the Jets. We are covering this over two parts, looking at NFC teams last week and AFC teams today. Every AFC team currently has at least one former Jet on it apart from the Denver Broncos. As ever, this list is intended to be exhaustive, but if we missed anyone, let us know in the comments. Bills: The Bills still have running back Ty Johnson under contract after he had been a solid third down back for them in recent years. Also on offense, Buffalo has three ex-Jets receivers but they are all probably long shots to make the team. Mecole Hardman was signed to a futures deal at the end of last season while Mac Dalena and Quentin Skinner were each picked up after the Jets released them recently. On defense, they re-signed defensive tackle Phidarian Mathis to compete for a role and linebacker Jimmy Ciarlo is back after contributing on special teams last year. Dolphins: After a solid 2025 season, Miami opted to keep ex-Jets placekicker Riley Patterson , clearing a path for Jason Sanders to end up with the Jets. They also have former preseason standout Donovan Edwards at running back and offensive tackle Carter Warren is also with the team but he is already on injured reserve. They cut ties with tight end Zack Kuntz, who ended up in Las Vegas. Patriots: New England made a splash by signing guard Alijah Vera-Tucker during the offseason and, if he makes it to the regular season, he could end up starting alongside one of his old teammates in Morgan Moses . The Patriots also retained defensive tackle Leonard Taylor III after he contributed to their postseason success last year. Bengals: Cincinnati has two former Jets quarterbacks batting to be the number two behind Joe Burrow, as they added Josh Johnson and re-signed Joe Flacco . Defensive back Ja’Sir Taylor is also now with the Bengals after being with the Jets for the second half of last season. Browns: Cleveland picked up former Jets linebacker Quincy Williams in free agency and he should start for them. Two other former Jets – tight end Brenden Bates and wide receiver Malachi Corley – will also compete for a roster spot. Ravens: Baltimore’s only ex-Jets player is currently guard John Simpson who is expected to start for them. Steelers: After much deliberation, the Steelers did eventually opt to re-sign quarterback Aaron Rodgers , who will reunite with defensive back Brandin Echols on the main roster. Wide receiver Brandon Smith and linebacker Jamin Davis are also with the team in training camp, but they released offensive lineman Calvin Anderson. Texans: Houston re-signed Sheldon Rankins after he played well for them last season and also added two former Jets to their special teams unit: Punter Kai Kroeger and return specialist Brandon Codrington . Colts: After their blockbuster trade somewhat backfired last season, the Colts will be hoping to see cornerback Sauce Gardner at his best in 2026. Indianapolis also signed defensive lineman Micheal Clemons to a three-year deal worth almost $6 million per season. Another defensive lineman, Derrick Nnadi was also brought in to compete and kicker Spencer Shrader is battling with Blake Grupe for a role. Titans: Robert Saleh is leaning on familiar faces as, by our count, the Titans have an incredible 12 ex-Jets on their roster right now, including six defensive linemen. Not all of these were Jets while Saleh was coaching, though, to be fair. That defensive line includes Jermaine Johnson , John Franklin-Myers and Solomon Thomas . Further depth comes from Jacob Martin , Jalyn Holmes and the most recent signing Khalen Saunders . At safety, Tony Adams previously started for Saleh, so he has a shot at a key role. Cornerback Mario Goodrich is more of a long-shot though. It’s possible none of their four offensive players that are former Jets will make the roster. These include running back Michael Carter , offensive linemen Austin Deculus , wide receiver Lance McCutcheon and quarterback Hendon Hooker . Jaguars: Jacksonville will get some offensive line depth from two former Jets in Chuma Edoga and Trystan Colon . They also added defensive back and special teamer Corey Ballentine . Broncos: As noted, this is the only NFL team without any ex-Jets players currently on it. Chargers: The Chargers re-signed linebacker Del’Shawn Phillips , who continues to be a special teams standout, to a two-year deal. Raiders: The only former Jets player on the Raiders’ roster is tight end Zack Kuntz , who was picked up after Miami let him go. Chiefs: Finally, the Chiefs’ most significant former Jets player is quarterback Justin Fields , who was acquired by trade but doesn’t look likely to get an opportunity with Patrick Mahomes already back on the practice field. Offensive tackle Esa Pole and wide receiver Jason Brownlee return from last year’s team and defensive back Tanner McCalister was a recent addition. We’ll be back after preseason with a look at which players made the final roster, or ended up in new homes…

Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: Jalen Hurts looked sharp – BGN JALEN HURTS UPDATE: Hurts looked pretty sharp today! QB1 completed all of his attempts in 7-on-7 … save for one dropped pass by E.J. Jenkins that hit the tight end in his hands. Hurts connected with Dallas Goedert over the middle with a ball that was placed just over the flyswatter dummy that’s designed to simulate a leaping defensive lineman. Hurts threw a perfect pass with anticipation into a tight window along the left sideline down the field to Dontayvion Wicks. Unlike earlier in his career, Hurts also doesn’t really take off running in 7-on-7, which is refreshing to see since that’s a useless thing to do in a pure passing drill. 7 standout players from NFL training camp so far – SB Nation Jalyx Hunt, EDGE — Philadelphia Eagles. The Eagles have so much defensive talent, and while Jalyx Hunt made a strong impression in limited time during the 2025 season, he’s really asserting himself now as a player to watch. Hunt has been blowing past the Eagles’ stout offensive line in practice and looking every bit of a double-digit sack guy, which is huge after Philly lost Jaelan Phillips in free agency. Seven takeaways from Vic Fangio’s Wednesday training camp press conference – PhillyVoice Vic likes what he has seen from Andrew Mukuba mentally so far. “It’s just experience, knowledge and know-how of the defense, Fangio said of the difference between Mukuba this year and last year. “You might look and say, ‘Man, he looks quicker. He’s in better shape. This, that.’ I think it’s just the thought process [speeding] up, comfortability with the defense and what he has to do. He’s in a little bit better shape too.” #JimmySays: I haven’t often seen Mukuba beaten through the first six practices. He is having a sneaky-good camp, in sort of a quiet way. How Eli Stowers is dealing with a slow start in his first NFL training camp – NBCSP One of the most important skills for a young rookie trying to find his way in the NFL is dealing with frustration. Dealing with disappointment. Dealing with the rough days that inevitably occur. For Eli Stowers, it’s all a part of football. “It’s always a challenge when something bad goes down, and you just have to continuously learn how to get back up, not worry about the last play and continue on to the next play,” Stowers said after practice Wednesday. I’m just out here trying to learn, continuously learn every single day. And I’m really appreciative of my coaches so far just trying to help me get going at this level and I’m super excited for what’s going to come.” Eagles training camp: Markel Bell works through ‘growing pains’ filling in for Lane Johnson – The Athletic The third-round rookie’s progress appears to be back on track. Bell initially filled in at right tackle during OTAs for Lane Johnson, who regularly misses the voluntary workouts to train on his own. Fred Johnson’s Saturday spot “start” suggested Bell still needed to improve. Bell said Lane Johnson told him “the other week” that there would be “growing pains” in learning the system and playing right tackle. Bell had only played left tackle in college. He acknowledged “it’s a whole different ballgame over there” and that he’s had to adjust against a defense that has ranked in the top nine in terms of EPA in both years under coordinator Vic Fangio. More than a week into Eagles training camp, Jalen Hurts and the new-look offense are ‘calibrating’ – Inquirer The new-look offense under first-year coordinator Sean Mannion is still in the early days of installation. While it got the best of Vic Fangio’s defense Monday, the defense has the upper hand so far through six days of practice. Wednesday’s practice was a run-heavy day, and it was a shorter practice compared to Tuesday’s session that ran nearly two hours. For Hurts, Wednesday was another chance to “continue to take strides.” It isn’t supposed to be easy to install a new offense against one of the best defenses in the NFL. “I like to think of the term calibrating,” Hurts said. “This is a time where we’re kind of putting it together and finding out who we are. We’ve got a lot of new pieces, an entirely new approach and MO, philosophy, to our offense. Being able to put that together and make it our own, I’m excited about where we are.” Spadaro: Marcus Epps takes Andrew Mukuba under his wing – PhiladelphiaEagles.com There has always been, in many instances, a big brother/little brother element in the Eagles’ locker room, a key to the team’s success through the years. When the veterans on the team care enough and are selfless enough to show younger players the way, transitions happen, careers are grown, seamless production takes place. Zach Ertz to Dallas Goedert … Jason Kelce to Cam Jurgens … Fletcher Cox to Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter … Darius Slay to Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean. The list goes on and on, and it is a huge reason why the Eagles have been a championship contender for so many seasons. There are similar stories happening now, and one of them is Marcus Epps and Andrew Mukuba. Epps is the eight-year veteran whose career has never been on a linear path – a sixth-round draft pick in Minnesota in 2019 who was released midway through his rookie season, picked up by the Eagles and a contributing player on the defense through the 2022 campaign, another move to Las Vegas for 2023 and 2024 before suffering a torn ACL, signed in New England for five months in early 2025, added to the Eagles’ practice squad last season, promoted to the 53-man roster in late September … A lot of moves. Nothing given. Everything earned. Lane Johnson misses fourth straight Eagles practice – PFT The Eagles are practicing without right tackle Lane Johnson for the fourth straight day on Wednesday. Johnson has been excused from practice for what is described as a non-injury related reason. There’s been no word from the team about when Johnson will be back, but Jeff McLane of the Philadelphia Inquirer reports that he is expected to return soon. 2026 NFL season: Future Hall of Famers from all 32 teams – ESPN Keep it up: QB Jalen Hurts, CB Quinyon Mitchell. I thought the Prescott Hall of Fame discussion was going to be tough. Hurts has obviously had rough points at times over the past few years, but he has also done two things the Hall of Fame loves: play quarterback and win a lot of games. Hurts is 57-25 as a starter and has two trips to the Super Bowl, winning the game’s MVP award when the Eagles blew out the Chiefs. He also finished second in regular-season MVP balloting to Patrick Mahomes in 2022, with a late-season shoulder injury costing Hurts a chance at taking home the hardware. The 2026 season feels critical for Hurts, who lost A.J. Brown during the offseason before a move to a new offensive system under Sean Mannion. If he…

title: Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: Jalen Hurts looked sharp
summary: Today marked the sixth Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES UP NEXT: The Eagles have a walkthrough closed to media access on Thursday. They’ll return to practice on Friday at 10:00 AM Eastern.
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JULY 30: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on during training camp at Jefferson Health Training Complex on July 30, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Today marked the sixth Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Here’s what I observed at the Jefferson Health Training Complex! EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES Today was a lighter day of practice. No pads. 75 minutes long. EAGLES INJURY UPDATES: BGN’s Alexis Chassen wrote up a comprehensive Eagles training camp injury report . The highlights: still no Lane Johnson (excused/not injury related), DeVonta Smith (hamstring), or Makai Lemon. Also, Landon Dickerson (rest/not injury related) sat out of practice for the first time this summer. JALEN HURTS UPDATE: Hurts looked pretty sharp today! QB1 completed all of his attempts in 7-on-7 … save for one dropped pass by E.J. Jenkins that hit the tight end in his hands. Hurts connected with Dallas Goedert over the middle with a ball that was placed just over the flyswatter dummy that’s designed to simulate a leaping defensive lineman. Hurts threw a perfect pass with anticipation into a tight window along the left sideline down the field to Dontayvion Wicks. Unlike earlier in his career, Hurts also doesn’t really take off running in 7-on-7, which is refreshing to see since that’s a useless thing to do in a pure passing drill. In 11-on-11, Hurts ripped a ball to Elijah Moore on a curl for a short gain. Hurts almost had a deep touchdown to Darius Cooper … but the second-year wide receiver couldn’t secure the ball that hit him in the hands as he was going to the ground. Would’ve been a tough grab but Hurts did his part to give Cooper a chance for the score. Stock up. Jalen Hurts singled out Darius Cooper when asked about the Eagles' wide receiver room. pic.twitter.com/Kt1moWHCUs — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) August 5, 2026 Drew Kendall took first-team left guard reps with Dickerson resting. Markell Bell continued to work at first-team right tackle with Lane Johnson not practicing. Jihaad Campbell broke up a pass in front of him meant for Samari Toure. Later, Campbell was flagged for defensive pass interference while covering Tank Bigsby. Speaking of Bigsby, it sure seems like he’s seen a lot of targets. BACKUP QUARTERBACK BATTLE: Tanner McKee was first up as QB2 in 7-on-7 but Andy Dalton took the first 11-on-11 series with the second-team offense. One of McKee’s best passes was a throw over the middle to Stone Smart … who had a really bad drop. Dalton hit a crossing Johnny Wilson (Dalton really likes throwing to him) in stride for a chunk gain. Dalton also hit a crossing Cam Latu in stride. Dalton did overthrow Danny Gray in the end zone to the right side. All told, Dalton has outplayed McKee in camp so far. Of course, still plenty of summer left to go. Arnold Ebiketie beat Fred Johnson to notch a “sack.” I tend to think the Eagles will keep Big Fred on the roster … but I don’t think he’s had a very good summer. I’ve been wondering if he’s a surprise cut candidate but he already has a $1.4 million guaranteed salary this season. The Eagles could trade him to clear $1.3 million in cap space with only $160,000 in dead money. Johnson could be made expendable if Bell proves to earn the coaching staff’s trust and, say, John Ojukwu emerges as a depth tackle option. The Eagles’ second-team offensive line: LT Fred Johnson, LG Jake Majors, C Willie Lampkin, RG Michael Jordan, RT John Ojukwu. It seems like Lampkin is climbing up the depth chart after previously repping on the third-team offensive line. Really interested to see him in preseason action. Grant Calcaterra had a ball bounce off his hands for a drop. Elijah Mitchell caught my eye multiple times today. He looked physical and eager for contact in pass protection against Jeremiah Trotter Jr. Mitchell also had a long run and he caught a pass from McKee in the flat for a good catch-and-run. Dameon Pierce also had a long run. Some good competition going on for RB4. (Or RB3?). Ambry Thomas got shook badly on a play where Quez Watkins made a short catch and juked the cornerback. The Eagles re-signed Brandon Hayes to help fill wide receiver reps due to multiple injuries. Hayes, perhaps shaking off some rust, dropped a pass from Dalton. Cole Payton threw another interception today. The rookie quarterback targeted Samari Toure over the middle but the ball was tipped into the air and caught by Tariq Castro-Fields. I much prefer Payton to be fearless than to look too scared to pull the trigger. That being said, Payton probably has to reign the aggression in a bit as he develops. Payton did connect with a crossing Erik Ezukanma in stride with a throw over the middle. Jeremy Maclin attended today’s practice. The former Eagles wide receiver has been the head coach of Kirkwood High School in Missouri since 2021. UP NEXT: The Eagles have a walkthrough closed to media access on Thursday. They’ll return to practice on Friday at 10:00 AM Eastern.

title: Vic Fangio says you shouldn’t sleep on this Eagles linebacker
summary: The Eagles were back on the practice field Wednesday, and defensive coordinator Vic Fangio spoke to reporters before things got started. He talked about Jordan Davis’ development as a pass rusher, and what he’s seen from some of the depth players, especially at linebacker. Here’s what the DC had to say: On Jordan Davis’ development […]
full_text: The Eagles were back on the practice field Wednesday, and defensive coordinator Vic Fangio spoke to reporters before things got started. He talked about Jordan Davis’ development as a pass rusher, and what he’s seen from some of the depth players, especially at linebacker. Here’s what the DC had to say: On Jordan Davis’ development Fangio was asked about how DT Jordan Davis has developed as a pass rusher, and the DC pointed to Davis’ physical changes. “Well, it first started at the end of the 2024 season. He got in better shape. He’s a much better pass rusher in the 330s than he is what he was, and that to me is the biggest thing.” He went on to explain that Davis needs to be his full 6-foot-6 when it’s to his advantage, but he also needs to bend his knees and be 6-foot-3 at times, which is easier to do when he weighs less and is in better shape. Being able to do move around easier and for a longer duration of time is what really propelled Davis’ game. Individual assessments OLB Arnold Ebiketie “He’s made nice progress here. I think coming in on the offseason, in the six OTAs that we had, it was kind of new to him. He was hesitant, not sure. I think he’s made a lot of progress in that manner, and is having a much better camp. Him, and some of the other guys are taking advantage of the reps their gaining with [Jonathan] Greenard being out for awhile.” DB Michael Carter “Right now, I feel good about him playing nickel, playing safety if need be. Maybe some of the other DBs in that bag, not so yet, but doesn’t mean they won’t get there. We don’t have a lot of new, young players on defense, so most of the guys that are here, have some background with us. So, we should be able to make those decisions a little quicker.” LB Chance Campbell “Don’t sleep on Chance [Campbell], now. You guys when you make your lists out there. We like Chance. Chance — he’s a good football player. Had some injuries earlier in his career that set him back, but since the day we picked him up last year, he’s shown that he’s a football player, and we like him. Interesting, last year, we picked him up the last week of the preseason game — I don’t remember the exact day, but it was just a few days before the game, and he didn’t need that acclimation period.“ LB Jeremiah Trotter “Trot’s had a very good camp. Trot, to me, along the same lines as we talked about with [Andrew] Mukuba — looking better, moving better, playing better. And I just think it’s not so much a conditioning and physical thing, it’s more of a knowing what he’s doing, seeing things quicker, faster, and playing faster. But, he’s had an excellent camp. It’s the best I’ve seen him look since we’ve had him.” Other notables Fangio talked a bit about how it’s difficult to balance getting starters reps while also keeping them healthy. And while they are committed to the development of the young players and new players, they aren’t prioritizing that over what’s best for the team and where the reps need to be. The DC says he hasn’t learned much about the Eagles new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and his play-calling style yet, noting that even though they’ve gone against each other in practice, there’s no scoreboard and it’s not a real game. “I wouldn’t be worried. And like I told [Sean Mannion], we obviously got the best of yesterday’s practice by a long shot, but that’s the way it’s been the last two years in training camp, the defense has gotten the best of the offense. So, not to be too concerned.” He did say that the new Eagles offensive style gives them some more opportunities to prepare for different teams they see throughout the season — especially as Jalen Hurts does more things under center. Fangio admitted it gives the defense more variety in practice than they’ve had the past few years. The DC talked about how the whole league is playing a lot more nickel, for many reasons, the biggest being the fullback position disappearing from offenses and being replaced by a third wideout or tight end. He noted that the Eagles played a lot of nickel in 2024 because he felt that was the best way to get their best players on the field. But, Fangio has a sense that things are reverting back a little bit, so there’s a chance that there’s more base defense this year by the Eagles and others around the league.

title: Eagles training camp injury updates
summary: It didn’t take long, but we’ve reached the point of Philadelphia Eagles training camp where a successful day is one with no injuries. That wasn’t the case on Tuesday and Wednesday. Perhaps most concerning was Cooper DeJean being sidelined with an arm injury on Tuesday. It wasn’t something that appeared concerning after being looked at […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - AUGUST 01: Philadelphia Eagles cornerback Cooper DeJean #33 is shown during the Philadelphia Eagles training camp on August 1st, 2026 at Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It didn’t take long, but we’ve reached the point of Philadelphia Eagles training camp where a successful day is one with no injuries. That wasn’t the case on Tuesday and Wednesday. Perhaps most concerning was Cooper DeJean being sidelined with an arm injury on Tuesday. It wasn’t something that appeared concerning after being looked at by the trainers. Thankfully, he was back on the field Wednesday. Wide receiver/return specialist Britain Covey also left Tuesday’s practice early. He didn’t practice on Wednesday due to a hamstring injury. He’s now the third receiver to deal with a hammy issue — joining both DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon , who missed practice entirely Tuesday and Wednesday. This now looks problematic for the rookie Lemon, who missed the last two weeks of OTAs after pulling a hamstring, and has now missed his third training camp practice in a row for the same thing. Reports suggest the team isn’t concerned about it, but it’s still not ideal for a young player to miss so many valuable reps. Lane Johnson missed Saturday’s practice with an “excused (not injury related)” designation, but it wasn’t announced why he was away. That mystery continued into mid-week, with the Eagles RT still not returning to training camp. Jeff McLane reported that Johnson was expected to return soon. Hopefully, he has the time and space for whatever he’s dealing with — and hopefully he’s able to get back soon, because after his injury last season and having to work with a new OL coach on a new scheme, this time is valuable. title: Steelers’ Joey Porter ranked outside top 25 NFL cornerbacks
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers continue to view Joey Porter Jr. as a potential cornerstone of their defense, but a new set of rankings suggests not everyone is as high on the former second-round pick. Bleacher Report’s NFL Scouting Department ranked Porter as the 27th-best cornerback in the NFL entering the 2026 season, placing him between Minnesota Vikings corner Byron Murphy […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - NOVEMBER 02: Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. (24) looks on during the NFL football game between the Indianapolis Colts and Pittsburgh Steelers on November 02, 2025 at Acrisure Stadium in Pittsburgh, PA. (Photo by Mark Alberti/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers continue to view Joey Porter Jr. as a potential cornerstone of their defense, but a new set of rankings suggests not everyone is as high on the former second-round pick. Bleacher Report’s NFL Scouting Department ranked Porter as the 27th-best cornerback in the NFL entering the 2026 season, placing him between Minnesota Vikings corner Byron Murphy Jr. at No. 26 and Philadelphia Eagles defensive back Riq Woolen at No. 28. The list is topped by Denver Broncos star Patrick Surtain II, widely regarded as one of the league’s premier shutdown corners. The ranking is likely to spark debate among Steelers fans, many of whom believe Porter has already established himself as one of the AFC’s better young cover corners. Since entering the league in 2023, Porter has consistently drawn difficult assignments against opposing No. 1 receivers while developing into a physical press-man defender capable of limiting explosive plays. While Porter has not always produced eye-catching interception totals, his ability to stay attached in coverage and challenge receivers at the line of scrimmage has made him one of Pittsburgh’s most trusted defensive backs. Given that reputation, a ranking outside the league’s top 25 cornerbacks may come as a surprise. The timing is also noteworthy as Porter continues to await a long-term contract extension from the Steelers. With several young cornerbacks around the league signing lucrative new deals, Pittsburgh faces increasing pressure to secure one of its defensive building blocks before his price climbs even higher. Every evaluation — whether favorable or critical — adds another layer to the discussion surrounding what Porter could ultimately command on his next contract. Whether Bleacher Report’s evaluation proves accurate or serves as added motivation, Porter will have an opportunity to change the narrative this season. A standout 2026 campaign against the NFL’s top receivers could quickly move him up future rankings while strengthening his case for one of the league’s richest contracts at the position. title: What we learned from attending Wednesday’s Seahawks training camp practice
summary: The Seattle Seahawks are in the middle of their second week of training camp as they gear up for another Super Bowl run. Field Gulls was on-site for Wednesday’s non-padded practice at the VMAC in Renton, plus we got to have a great chat with Emerald City Spectrum’s Corbin Smith as part of our special […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks are in the middle of their second week of training camp as they gear up for another Super Bowl run. Field Gulls was on-site for Wednesday’s non-padded practice at the VMAC in Renton, plus we got to have a great chat with Emerald City Spectrum’s Corbin Smith as part of our special Seahawks Syndicate live post-practice podcast . Thursday is a glorified walkthrough for the Seahawks, so this is essentially an “off-day” for us before Friday and Saturday practices. In the meantime, I’ve emptied my notebook with a deeper summary of what we saw at Wednesday’s practice, along with some extra podcast insight from Corbin as a longtime credentialed Seahawks reporter. The Sam Darnold to Rashid Shaheed connection is legit and it’s growing I would not call Wednesday’s practice a great day for the offense; Drew Lock and the second unit probably fared the best in 11-on-11s. However, we want give-and-take and for both units to sharpen each other up, so please don’t fret too much. If you want to get excited about something, it’s the Darnold to Shaheed combo. Shaheed ran an over route to the right sideline and Darnold lobbed the ball perfectly to Rashid for an explosive play. Shaheed also made a great hands-only catch along the sideline with Josh Jobe (I think, it could’ve been Nehemiah Pritchett but I didn’t write it down) draped all over him. Shaheed shouldn’t be typecast as a deep threat and he won’t be in this offense. Seattle worked on getting him the ball on a screen pass in the red zone, on intermediate-ish throws over the middle, so there’s room to grow in Shaheed’s first camp with the Super Bowl champs. Jalen Milroe is getting more put on his plate Please do not conflate the sub-headline with the idea that he’s set to even overtake Drew Lock on the depth chart this season. What I mean by that is Milroe is not predominantly parked in shotgun and throwing to guys who have no functional shot to make the roster. Brian Fleury has Milroe getting plays in with Elijah Arroyo and Jadarian Price, who have worked with the first- through third-team offense. We’ll be here for two more practices, so I’ll have a more definitive assessment on his performances after Saturday. Any thought of the Milroe package returning this year is contingent on Milroe being a threat as a passer. Brian Fleury all but hinted at that in his press conference on Tuesday. What I’m looking for in preseason is for Milroe to maybe get a few snaps with the second-team offense and to show enough for the staff to be confident that, if he has the odd snap in a regular season game, it is not an immediate tell that it’s just a QB run or option play. Pass protection is a work in progress for the non-George Holani running backs Seattle’s pass pro standouts at the running back position are George Holani (whom Corbin called ‘Furious George’ for his style) and Zach Charbonnet. One of these guys is not playing for another several weeks. Jadarian Price, Emanuel Wilson, and Velus Jones Jr collectively are not as good as either Holani or Charbonnet in pass pro. Price has a lot of time on his side to get better but I noticed how much Thomas Hammock was coaching him up during pass pro drills and having him re-do his reps. The lack of history of pass pro and pass catching at Notre Dame means Price still has a lot to learn. Velus Jones is a receiver/running back hybrid so a lot of this is new to him. Wilson is probably okay without being outstanding. I think that RB pass pro is a reasonable concern for Seattle to have entering the regular season, but I also want to see what happens the rest of this week and in preseason. Speaking of Charbonnet, by the way… Zach Charbonnet’s return timeline looks promising We saw Zach Charbonnet at practice not just walking normally, but also doing some ramp-up activities like one-legged jumping. One of Corbin’s tidbits from last night’s show was telling us that Charbonnet is both walking and running “perfectly normal” and from what he’s seen, he believes Charbonnet will be off PUP and ready to play Week 5 against the San Francisco 49ers. The important thing to note about the PUP list this year is that players can now have their practice window open up as early as the start of Week 3 instead of Week 4, so that will be the litmus test for Charbonnet’s readiness. It’s going to come down to the wire for that sixth wide receiver spot I believe the Seahawks will roster six wide receivers this season. We can checkmark Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Tory Horton, Rashid Shaheed, Cooper Kupp (who had a vet rest day and barely practiced), and Jake Bobo as the top five. For WR6? Whoo boy it’s going to be fun. Cody White is Cody White and I mean that endearingly. He’s a workmanlike player who seems to be getting better as a receiver, plus he has special teams value. Ricky White III, perhaps in part because Jake Bobo is hurt, is stepping up and earning more reps with the second-team offense and has shown smooth route-running and good hands. Montorie Foster, whose practice inauspiciously started by muffing a punt in punt return drills, had a few bright moments mostly working with the threes and Jalen Milroe. Emmanuel Henderson got involved a little bit but I think his route is realistically on special teams. This will be a battle that will go through the end of preseason. Anthony Bradford is not losing his starting job, deal with it Sorry if I sound coarse but I’m also being realistic. Beau Stephens is an awesome hype man but he’s still a fifth-round rookie who is currently running with the third-team offense. That’s right. Christian Haynes has been with the second-team offense consistently, and he has no shot to usurp Bradford. This means that for the first time in his career, Bradford doesn’t have to battle to earn his job. If he has an indefensibly bad string of regular season performances, perhaps we can revisit this convo. But for now, there is no starting RG competition for Week 1. Incidentally, Stephens had a big wrap on his left arm (thanks to Bryce Coutts for noticing that, hence he is “The Hawks Eye” podcast host ), which suggested injury, but he practiced the whole way. Corbin said it’s the first time he’s seen it so it looks to be a new issue. Rylie Mills is going to have a major role on Seattle’s defense He lines up as a big end, he lines up as a 3-technique, he lines up sometimes at nose, he is a big, strong, versatile human being whose Super Bowl sack only scratched the surface of what he’s capable of. Mills blew up pass plays on the first- and second-team units and wins with power, hand fighting, and out-leveraging his man. I can’t wait to see him in a padded practice. The one thing I’d say is I back him to be more of a pass rusher than top run defender, but that’s just instinct more than anything else. The camp hype is real. The deeper EDGE depth was underwhelming I specify “deeper” as anyone below Dante Fowler Jr on the depth chart. Aidan Hubbard, Jalan Gaines, Jared Ivey (who didn’t practice), Connor O’Toole, and Marvin Jones Jr are the bottom-end of the EDGE group. Gaines had a nice play in which he snuffed out a Drew Lock play-action and would’ve had a sack at normal game speed, and I think Marvin Jones would’ve been credited with a coverage sack on another 11-on-11 rep. That’s about it. In previous practice write-ups from beat reporters there have been scant mentions of any of the fringe edge rushers standing out and making a push to be on the 53. Corbin told us that Hubbard, “looked like he’s playing in slow motion.” Watching him in camp that looked to be the case. Seattle was fortunate enough to have none of its core edge rushers miss more than a game here and there, because anything beyond that and I’d have some concern. However, this is Mike Macdonald, and he has some ideas… Tyrice Knight, living on the “edge”? It sounds like Tyrice Knight has had a good training camp, and the third-year linebacker had a few splash plays in coverage on Wednesday, including a…

title: Why Grey Zabel’s rookie film suggests he’s one of John Schneider’s best first-round value picks
summary: The Seattle Seahawks’ first-round history under John Schneider has never been boring. Over the years, the Seahawks have used premium draft capital on prospects who divided evaluators, while other first-round picks have been moved in aggressive trades for established veterans. That willingness to trust the organization’s board over public consensus has produced both memorable successes […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - DECEMBER 07: Grey Zabel #76 of the Seattle Seahawks drops back to block during an NFL football game against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on December 7, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks’ first-round history under John Schneider has never been boring. Over the years, the Seahawks have used premium draft capital on prospects who divided evaluators, while other first-round picks have been moved in aggressive trades for established veterans. That willingness to trust the organization’s board over public consensus has produced both memorable successes and frustrating misses. One year into Grey Zabel’s NFL career, however, it’s becoming increasingly difficult not to view him as one of the best first-round values of Schneider’s tenure. Background Coming out of North Dakota State, Zabel entered the draft process with two primary concerns attached to his scouting report. The first was his arm length. For teams projecting him as an NFL tackle, his measurements created understandable questions. Seattle, however, drafted him with the expectation that his future would likely come inside at guard, where his technical ability, leverage and movement skills matter far more than a few inches of reach. The second concern was the level of competition. Dominating FCS opponents doesn’t always translate to Sundays, making the transition from North Dakota State to the NFL one of the biggest unknowns surrounding his projection. Ironically, Zabel began answering those questions long before he ever played an NFL snap. A quick side note: I’ve become a huge believer in the value of the Senior Bowl. Maybe that’s because Seattle consistently finds contributors through the event, but I also appreciate prospects who embrace the entire process instead of leaving after one or two impressive practice sessions. Zabel embodied exactly what the Senior Bowl is supposed to showcase. Throughout the week he accepted every challenge presented to him, taking reps at multiple interior positions while competing against some of the best defensive linemen in the country. He didn’t manage his workload, didn’t leave early and finished the week by playing in the game itself. Combined with his decision to stay at North Dakota State for his final collegiate season instead of transferring to a larger program, it reinforced the type of competitor Seattle was drafting. That mentality quickly carried over into his rookie season. Despite suffering an injury against the Los Angeles Rams that initially looked serious enough to cost him time, Zabel returned remarkably quickly. He clearly wasn’t operating at full strength against the Titans the following week, but simply getting back onto the field that soon spoke volumes about both his toughness and determination. Like every rookie offensive lineman, his season wasn’t flawless. Seattle’s offensive line experienced its share of growing pains throughout the year, and Zabel had his own moments of inconsistency. Even so, his overall body of work consistently pointed toward a player whose strengths translated immediately to the NFL. What stood out on tape Elite footwork/Athletic Ability If there is one trait that consistently jumps off the tape, it’s Zabel’s footwork. Zabel's footwork consistently stands out. While many rookie OL are still working through their kick step, he's often already on his third, staying square, recovering against counters and reaching landmarks before defenders can exploit leverage. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:06:57.740Z One of the biggest differences between him and many rookie offensive linemen is how quickly he gets himself into position. While some blockers are still working through their initial kick step, Zabel is often already on his third step, allowing him to stay square, recover against counters and reach landmarks before defenders can exploit leverage. Grey Zabel's footwork is outstanding. He wastes no time climbing to the second level, takes the proper angle and removes the linebacker from the play before he has any chance to react. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:08:09.194Z Excellent footwork and nimble feet are traits that consistently show up on Grey Zabel’s tape. On this rep, he immediately climbs to the linebacker, reaches him without hesitation, and—unlike the previous snap—takes a much cleaner angle to completely erase any chance of the defender getting involved in the play. Elite mobility for an OL. Zabel locates his target at the third level, stays under control and sustains the block nearly 30 yards downfield, finishing the rep with the same intensity as the snap. PS: Amazing call from Klint Kubiak — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:09:24.214Z Outstanding mobility paired with the vision to locate and engage targets at the second and even third level. It’s rare to see an offensive lineman sustain blocks with this kind of control 30 yards downfield, but Zabel finishes the rep as if the play had just begun. Zabel's athleticism is on full display. He reaches the second level with almost no wasted movement, weaving through traffic under control. One of the cleanest and most impressive blocks on his 2025 tape. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:10:09.047Z Another example of the athleticism that makes Zabel such a unique prospect. Many offensive linemen can eventually reach the second level, but it often looks labored. Zabel gets there effortlessly, wasting virtually no movement as he flows through traffic. This was one of the most impressive blocking reps of his entire season. Promising technique Beyond his movement skills, Zabel consistently plays with refined technique. Zabel's hand usage, balance and control rarely look like those of a rookie. His tape shows steady growth throughout the season, even if inconsistency showed up at times—like allowing two sacks to Kobie Turner before bouncing back with quality reps. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:11:07.508Z His hand usage, balance and ability to stay under control rarely resemble those of a first-year player. More importantly, the tape suggests he became increasingly comfortable as the season progressed rather than maintaining the same level of play. Obviously, inconsistency will appear, like in this game where he allowed two sacks to Kobie Turner and in the same game had good snaps against him. Outstanding rep vs. the 49ers. Zabel absorbs a powerful bull rush, anchors despite the length disadvantage, then shuts down multiple counters with excellent balance, hand usage and recovery. High-level pass protection. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:11:50.813Z Outstanding rep against the 49ers. The defensive tackle attacks with power immediately off the snap, but Zabel absorbs the initial surge and anchors well. Despite giving up arm length, his hand placement and technical refinement allow him to maintain leverage and keep the pocket clean. After his initial rush stalls, the defender strings together multiple counters, but Zabel’s balance, hand usage, and recovery ability neutralize every one of them. Areas for improvement Most of Zabel’s negative plays weren’t the result of losing individual matchups. Instead, many of them reflected communication issues that affected Seattle’s offensive line throughout the season. This looks more like a protection breakdown than a physical loss. The left side slides to protect the outside gap, but Zabel loses track of his assignment, allowing No. 10 through almost untouched. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:13:18.861Z Several missed assignments involved double teams failing to climb properly to the second level, delayed handoffs between blockers or protection adjustments that never fully developed against stunts. The left side of the offensive line is clearly working to protect the outside gap, as shown by the center’s and left tackle’s initial…

full_text: The Seattle Seahawks held their seventh of 10 public training camp practices on Wednesday. It was another warm (and, due to the wildfire smoke, hazy) day at team headquarters in Renton, and the VMAC berm was filled to capacity yet again for what was a non-padded practice for the reigning Super Bowl champions. While the pads may not have been there, there was still a lot to take in. Field Gulls was on-site at VMAC observing what was just about a 2.5-hour long practice. Myself and fellow Field Gulls staff writer and host of The Hawks Eye podcast , Bryce Coutts, filmed a quick reaction video after practice ended (from outside The Pro Shop in Renton, we were in a hurry to get to SoDo!) with our immediate takeaways and analysis. Over a nice and tight five minutes, we discussed how well the defense performed, the Sam Darnold-Rashid Shaheed connection, an interesting name to watch at safety, Nehemiah Pritchett’s increased role with the starters, Rylie Mills’ versatility, and the work in progress that is a rebuilding running game. (Update: We’ve swapped in the video to include auto-generated and therefore not totally accurate transcription, so this should be a help!) They are already at Wednesday’s practice. In a corresponding move, cornerback Brandon Johnson and edge rusher Garrett Nelson were waived. Johnson had been with the team since mid-July, […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks announced a pair of signings on Wednesday afternoon, adding running back T.J. Harden and cornerback Jordan Washington, who both went undrafted earlier this year. They are already at Wednesday’s practice. In a corresponding move, cornerback Brandon Johnson and edge rusher Garrett Nelson were waived. Johnson had been with the team since mid-July, and Nelson signed on Tuesday. Across four years at UCLA, Harden totaled 1,658 rushing yards and 12 touchdowns, before transferring to SMU for his senior season. He continued to impress with the Mustangs, leading the team with 787 rushing yards, accompanied by 12 touchdowns. While it wasn’t enough to be drafted, he signed with the Cleveland Browns in May, before being waived on August 3. Washington, a familiar face, spent rookie camp with Seattle after going undrafted out of Stanford. Prior to transferring before his senior season, Washington played four seasons at Dartmouth where he recorded 72 tackles, 6.5 tackles for loss and 20 passes defended.

title: Sam Darnold continues remarkable ascent in The Athletic’s NFL QB Tiers survey
summary: Where does the Seattle Seahawks’ Super Bowl champion quarterback fit in the NFL’s landscape? A lot higher than he used to be. The Athletic’s Mike Sando compiles an annual survey of 50 coaches and executives to rank the starting quarterbacks (plus would-be young starters and lingering veterans who are borderline starters/backups) by tiers. A Tier […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - JANUARY 25: Sam Darnold #14 of the Seattle Seahawks celebrates after defeating the Los Angeles Rams an NFC Championship NFL football game at Lumen Field on January 25, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Where does the Seattle Seahawks’ Super Bowl champion quarterback fit in the NFL’s landscape? A lot higher than he used to be. The Athletic’s Mike Sando compiles an annual survey of 50 coaches and executives to rank the starting quarterbacks (plus would-be young starters and lingering veterans who are borderline starters/backups) by tiers. A Tier 1 quarterback is the best of the best, whereas a Tier 5 quarterback is is anywhere from an unknown to not a viable starter. The tier numbers (1, 2, 3, 4, and 5) are then averaged out and QBs are ranked accordingly by their average tier ranking, not where the evaluators would rank a QB as far as top five, top ten, etc. Sam Darnold has had to take the difficult road to work his way up the rankings. From purgatory with the New York Jets to the Lombardi Trophy with Seattle, Darnold has moved up a tier for a third consecutive year. His aggregate ranking is 14th, tied with Baker Mayfield. Check out some of the quotes: Darnold’s climb over the past three seasons is rare for an established starter in the 13-year history of QB Tiers. “Sam played his ass off the last two years,” a head coach said. Darnold’s improvement from 4.00 to 2.36 is a full tier better than runner-up Daniel Jones among the 19 quarterbacks who appeared in all three surveys and had debuted before 2024. […] “There are so many factors that determine a quarterback’s success, and Darnold’s the best example of it,” an exec said. “To get him into the right system, with the right coaches, and you have a game-breaking receiver, and a good defense. It’s a lot easier.” […] “Sam is at his best when you run the ball, play defense and then he’s not in position to turn the ball over,” an exec said, “but when his number is called, he can make big plays. If they don’t start running the football, they probably don’t win the Super Bowl.” For more context, a Tier 2 quarterback, “carries his team sometimes,” “handles pure-passing situations in doses or has other dimensions that elevate him above Tier 3,” and “has a hole or two in his game.” The Tier 2 range starts with Lamar Jackson at No. 5 and cuts off at Jalen Hurts at No. 17. The Tier 3 “Legit starter but needs better running game or defense to win” quarterback starts with Bo Nix and ends with the 2026 version of Kirk Cousins. The only Tier 1 QBs are Patrick Mahomes, Josh Allen, Matthew Stafford, and Joe Burrow. The one sort of critical remark re Darnold is not completely unfounded. Sando noted that Darnold has had the best support from his defense and special teams over the past two seasons, which means he’s been in one of the more optimal environments for a quarterback to succeed. The good news? He’s succeeding instead of dragging a talented team down. In many respects, this is not too dissimilar from Russell Wilson getting to benefit from an elite defense and special teams unit at the start of his career. It’s almost as if being good to great in all of the most important areas of football is extremely valuable, and putting everything on the QB’s plate is not optimal! I have no issue with Darnold’s tier ranking even if I’d separate the tie and put Darnold above Mayfield (who somehow got a Tier 1 vote). I’d also rank him above No. 11 Caleb Williams, who’s being over-stated in my opinion and we should probably wait a little bit to see if he can build on 2025 by not having to rely on so many improbable fourth quarter comebacks. Brock Purdy is still in Tier 2, which is totally fine when you consider he was an MVP finalist in 2023 and played well under difficult circumstances in 2025. Every Tier 1 or Tier 2 QB except Justin Herbert has at least won a playoff start, while 12 out of 17 have made a Conference Championship, and eight have reached a Super Bowl. These are the two tiers you want your QB to be in, otherwise you have functionally no shot at a championship run. Seattle is fortunate to have another Tier 1-2 quarterback to build around, and even if you think Darnold should individually be ranked higher within that specific tier, that he keeps improving his ranking is a sign of respect and acknowledgement of improvement from the league’s evaluators. In case you’re wondering, former Seahawks starter Geno Smith has plunged all the day down to Tier 4 (“Veteran who ideally would not be a full-season starter”) at No.30. summary: The San Francisco 49ers personnel department has been busy as they deal with having 20 players currently injured. According to Wednesday’s transaction wire, the team worked out several players before they signed wide receiver KhaDarel Hodge. The 49ers officially terminated a pair of vested veterans in Cam Sample and Kevin Givens. They were injured/waived. Here […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FL - OCTOBER 30:Miami Dolphins offensive tackle Kion Smith (71) goes to the locker room after pregame warmup before the game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Miami Dolphins on Thursday, October 30, 2025 at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, FL. (Photo by Peter Joneleit/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers personnel department has been busy as they deal with having 20 players currently injured . According to Wednesday’s transaction wire, the team worked out several players before they signed wide receiver KhaDarel Hodge. The 49ers officially terminated a pair of vested veterans in Cam Sample and Kevin Givens. They were injured/waived. Here is a list of players the 49ers worked out, not counting Hodge: OG Braden Daniels OT Ryan Mosesso OG Kion Smith WR Kristian Wilkerson WR Donovan Peoples-Jones The 49ers have been thin at wide receiver since the beginning of the week. Since the week began, offensive linemen Brett Toth had an undisclosed injury, while Carver Willis was in the concussion protocol. We will find out if the team adds one of the linemen ahead of practice. Daniels was drafted in the fourth round of the 2023 NFL Draft out of Utah. He was placed on the IR in August during his rookie year with a torn rotator cuff. He’s been on multiple practice squads, but has never played a regular-season snap. Mosesso was the starting right tackle for Massachusetts during the previous two seasons. The 6-foot-5, 305-pounder also has experience at guard and left tackle during his collegiate days. Smith has been in the NFL since 2021. He has 201 total snaps across that time, with 137 coming last year with the Miami Dolphins. He’s 6’6″, 300 pounds. For what it’s worth, he was the Dolphins’ opening-day starter in 2025 at right guard. Wilerson has been in the NFL since 2020. The 6’1″, 214-pound wide receiver was with the Raiders in 2023 and 2024. For his career, he has six receptions for 60 yards spread across four seasons. Peoples-Jones is a name everyone likely knows. He was with the Browns from 2020 through 2023. In 2022, Peoples-Jones had an 839-yard season. For his career, he has 122 receptions for 1,895 yards. His problem was always drops and a lack of separation. It seemed like Peoples-Jones didn’t know the playbook either, constantly lining up in the wrong spot during his days with the Browns. We’ll find out shortly if the 49ers add one of these players to the roster before Thursday’s practice. Kyle’s update, 9:52 a.m. PT: No surprise, as the 49ers made an official move to add a lineman. They signed Kion Smith. The corresponding move was to waive Colton Dowell. Smith started the first three games of the season for Miami last year at right guard. He was good for the first two games, but struggled in the third game against the Bills, based on his blown block rate.

title: 49ers trade for Falcons star in trade proposal ‘that makes too much sense’
summary: On Wednesday, the San Francisco 49ers continued to reunite defensive coordinator Raheem Morris with some of his former players, signing defensive lineman Ogbo Okoronkwo and wide receiver KhaDarel Hodge. Both veterans are coming into position groups in need of depth after the injury bug has hit the 49ers once again during training camp. Morris now […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - DECEMBER 29: Safety Jessie Bates III (3) of the Atlanta Falcons and the Falcons celebrate the pick 6 by safety Jessie Bates III (3) of the Atlanta Falcons during the first half of the Monday night NFL game between the Atlanta Falcons and the Los Angeles Rams on December 29, 2025 at the Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by David J. Griffin/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images On Wednesday, the San Francisco 49ers continued to reunite defensive coordinator Raheem Morris with some of his former players, signing defensive lineman Ogbo Okoronkwo and wide receiver KhaDarel Hodge . Both veterans are coming into position groups in need of depth after the injury bug has hit the 49ers once again during training camp. Morris now has a couple of familiar faces on defense, and ESPN’s latest trade proposal has him reuniting with another. ESPN’s Seth Walder conjured up five training camp trades that ‘make too much sense’, which include the 49ers trading a 2027 third-round pick for Atlanta Falcons star safety Jessie Bates and a 2028 sixth-round pick. Bates, 29, would provide an immediate upgrade at safety for the 49ers, who have struggled at the position in recent years with their young players being inconsistent. “The Falcons’ 2023 signing of Bates was an example of free agency gone right,” Walder wrote. “The Falcons paid sticker price — four years and $64 million — to sign Bates, who was very effective in Cincinnati and continued that quality play in Atlanta. That was particularly true in 2023, when Bates delivered six interceptions and three forced fumbles while earning second-team All-Pro honors. “He was good again in 2024, but he wasn’t quite on the same level last season. Still, the 29-year-old Bates remains one of the best safeties in the league. (He ranked fifth in this year’s survey of coaches and executives conducted by ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler).” For the Falcons, the move makes sense in a salary-shedding sense to push their chips towards the 2028 season and focus more on their younger players. “If the Falcons were expected to contend, it would make sense to keep Bates and see the original contract through,” Walder continued. “But they aren’t, and with a ton of 2027 cap space even after the Bijan Robinson extension, the Falcons will likely be spenders next offseason. They would risk losing Bates without getting a compensatory pick in return if he walks in free agency. So it’s better for Atlanta to deal him now. And while that would mean finding a replacement for Bates, the Falcons wouldn’t be lacking in safety talent thanks to emerging second-year player Xavier Watts. “It just so happens that former Falcons head coach Raheem Morris, who coached Bates the past two seasons, is now the 49ers’ defensive coordinator. And he could use an upgrade at safety alongside Ji’Ayir Brown and Malik Mustapha. The timing works, as the 49ers are contenders who could use defensive help after ranking 25th in EPA allowed per dropback last season. “San Francisco would be giving up real draft capital for a short-term player, but that’s an indicator of Bates’ skill and the fact that his contract would cost the 49ers only $13 million in 2026 — a below-market price to sign a player of his caliber.” This is the type of move we’ve seen happen at the deadline in years past, and the 49ers also haven’t invested much in the safety position. But the fit does make a lot of sense, given that Bates is still 29 and very familiar with Raheem Morris’s defense. San Francisco also still has plenty of cap space, and Bates is on the final year of his deal, set to make just over $13 million a year. If there’s a time to push the chips in, it would be now. But with the NFC South wide open in Kevin Stefanski’s first year at the helm, I’m not sure that Atlanta would trade Bates until the midseason mark.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 3: KhaDarel Hodge #12 of the Atlanta Falcons scores a game-winning touchdown during overtime of an NFL football game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 3, 2024 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images KhaDarel Hodge, another former Raheem Morris player, joins the 49ers “Hodge lined up primarily on the outside with the Falcons. While he’s likely nothing more than a camp body, that nugget is important as it would allow De’Zhaun Stribling, or maybe Deebo Samuel, or whichever player they want to focus on getting more slot reps. It’s going to be a critical couple of weeks for players like Jacob Cowing and Junior Bergen. Both are fighting for that final roster spot at wideout. They’ll need to show they can win inside and outside. It shouldn’t be ruled out that if both excel, Christian Kirk might be the odd man out, even if it’s because of an injury. It also helps, in Cowing’s case, that he has the upper hand at punt returner — for now, at least.” 49ers’ Dre Greenlaw opens up on lost season with Broncos: ‘Fighting demons left and right’ (paywall) “I don’t blame anything on the Broncos,” he said. “Coming off the Achilles and the calf (injuries), I just wasn’t in the shape that I needed to be to go out there with them and give it all I got. I should have taken it slow. (But) naturally, they’d just paid me, so that’s all I wanted to do — go show them what I could do. And it bit me in the ass, the second day I got there.” Similarly, Greenlaw owns his failure to master Joseph’s scheme. “I know what I could have done better, as far as being in that film,” he said. “That’s where I feel like I let myself and everybody down.” …“Dre, he grew up different, and I always felt like he thrived in San Francisco because he had the right group of people who he trusted,” Al-Shaair said. “When you’re used to doing things the same way for so long, and you’ve been exposed to that gold standard, it’s tough to break that — even if you go to a building where people are good at what they do.” 49ers interim head coach Chris Foerster shares Week 3 training camp updates “It seems like we’re very healthy. I mean, we have injuries. We have dings and bumps and bruises, and guys are missing practices. It’s yet to come up in anything I’ve heard. Doesn’t mean it hasn’t been discussed, but, shoot, I think it will be plenty. If you’re two deep at every position, you can practice. You can always adjust with the threes, one, two, threes. Threes are hard to stay healthy through the course of training camp, if you’re practicing football hard. If you’re not practicing football hard, you can get through camp easily without injuries, a couple muscles here and there. But if you’re practicing hitting, contact, style of football, whatever it is. So, yeah, that’s not come up at this point.” 49ers signing Ogbo Okoronkwo to bolster pass rush depth “Okoronkwo’s 2025 campaign was cut short after he suffered a season-ending triceps tear in Week 4. His last full season came in 2024 with the Browns, when he totaled 23 tackles, five tackles for loss, three sacks, and one forced fumble. Over two seasons in Cleveland, he recorded 7.5 sacks. His most productive season came in 2022 with the Texans, when he posted career highs with 44 tackles and five sacks. Across 81 career games (13 starts), Okoronkwo has compiled 132 tackles, 17 sacks, four forced fumbles, one fumble recovery, and four passes defensed.” The Good and Not So Good from Day 7 of 49ers Camp: Bosa and Greenlaw Miss a Day “By far the most physically gifted quarterback on the roster even though he’s the smallest quarterback on the roster. He’s just so quick and difficult to contain in the pocket, which is important for the 49ers, because they don’t provide much of a pocket. And when it’s time to throw, Purdy is making outstanding decisions with the ball. He hasn’t forced a pass into coverage in more than a week. Unfortunately for him, his best receiver remains his running back, and his best wide receiver currently is Jordan Watkins….Now that Mike Evans, Ricky Pearsall and Jacob Cowing are injured, the 49ers’ top-three healthy wide receivers on the depth chart are Demarcus Robinson, Deebo Samuel and Jordan Watkins. And today, the best of those three clearly was Watkins, who caught a deep touchdown pass from Purdy during 11-on-11s. Of these three healthy wide receivers, Watkins is the youngest, the fastest, the quickest, and the best route runner. He can beat you with a quick slant or a post over the top. The only area of the field where he struggles is over the middle, because he’s not particularly big. Still, he’s improving.” ESPN proposes 49ers trade for All-Pro safety Jessie Bates “They would risk losing Bates without getting a compensatory pick in return if he walks in free agency,” Walder added. “So it’s better for Atlanta to deal him now….San Francisco would be giving up real draft capital for a short-term player, but that’s an indicator of Bates’ skill and the fact that his contract would cost the 49ers only $13 million in 2026 — a below-market price to sign a player of his caliber,” Walder wrote.” Early 49ers training camp trends: CB, LB groups look fierce; DE already an issue (paywall) “ Thanks to newcomers Jack Jones, Nate Hobbs and rookie Ephesians Prysock, it’s a deep group. And it’s a group that’s being allowed to play to its feisty strength. The biggest critique of San Francisco’s defense in recent years is that it’s been too static and predictable. Robert Saleh, who implemented the system in 2017, preferred to keep things simple because he wanted his players to be fast and aggressive. ….A more aggressive style of cornerback play has been apparent in the first few practices. It’s a style that seems to fit starters Deommodore Lenoir, Renardo Green and Upton Stout, all of whom see themselves as “dogs” on defense. (Well, Lenoir sees himself as a hyena, which is doglike.)”
