title: 49ers’ Chris Foerster: ‘If you’re not practicing football hard, you can get through camp easily without injuries’
summary: Chris Foerster and the coaching staff have been tasked with managing the injuries for the San Francisco 49ers. Four players were added to the injury list ahead of Wednesday’s practice. If you include the players on the Injured Reserve, the Niners were without 23 players. That’s enough to field an offense and a defense. The […]
full_text: San Francisco 49ers acting head coach Chris Foerster during a news conference at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara on Sunday, July 26, 2026. Foerster is the assistant head coach and offensive line coach stepping in as acting head coach as Kyle Shanahan recovers from a car crash. (Photo by Santiago Mejia/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images) Chris Foerster and the coaching staff have been tasked with managing the injuries for the San Francisco 49ers. Four players were added to the injury list ahead of Wednesday’s practice. If you include the players on the Injured Reserve, the Niners were without 23 players. That’s enough to field an offense and a defense. The plan was to give Robert Jones and Carver Willis some work at left guard with the starters, while Connor Colby would play right guard. Unfortunately for Willis, he’s in the concussion protocol. Add in Brett Toth, and that meant Foerster didn’t have enough bodies to play musical chairs with the interior line on Wednesday. Foerster said, “I had a lot more in store,” but ultimately only ended up using Jones at left guard. Foerster was asked if the 49ers would need to cancel their joint practice next week. He said, “It’s yet to come up in anything I’ve heard. Doesn’t mean it hasn’t been discussed, but shoot, I think we’ll have plenty of players.” He understands that physicality is necessary to get your team ready for the regular season: “If you’re not practicing football hard, you can get through camp easily without injuries, a couple of muscles here and there. But if you’re practicing hitting, contact, style of football, whatever it is — so yeah, that’s not come up at this point.” Foerster made it sound like the team is taking caution with some of the injuries, as they should. For example, Trent Williams, who isn’t injured, is on a rep count. Foerster had a phenomenal quote that applies to every player: “You always have to be careful that reps in July don’t take away from reps in January.” Foerster continued, “It seems like we’re very healthy. I mean, we have injuries. We have dings and bumps and bruises, and guys are missing practices. If you have two deep at every position, you can practice. You can always adjust with the threes. One, two, threes. Threes are hard to stay healthy through the course of training camp if you’re practicing football hard.” The 49ers have adjusted their practice schedule to avoid injuries. The league even mandated specific days off so teams aren’t practicing consecutive days in a row. Yet, despite the 49ers not having double-digit practices yet, nearly a quarter of their team has “dings and bumps and bruises.”
author: Kyle Posey

title: Deebo Samuel on 49ers return: ‘It was a matter of time’
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have done their best at reuniting with past players before Week 1 of the 2026 season. LB Dre Greenlaw is back after one season with the Denver Broncos, and WR Deebo Samuel is back following his lone season in Washington. Greenlaw’s return is exciting as he will pair again with Fred […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 30: Deebo Samuel Sr. #1 of the San Francisco 49ers warms up before the game against the Detroit Lions at Levi's Stadium on December 30, 2024 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers have done their best at reuniting with past players before Week 1 of the 2026 season. LB Dre Greenlaw is back after one season with the Denver Broncos, and WR Deebo Samuel is back following his lone season in Washington. Greenlaw’s return is exciting as he will pair again with Fred Warner, but Samuel’s return is out of pure necessity and is a pivot from the 49ers’ original plan for the offense. Ricky Pearsall is done for the season. Mike Evans and D’Zhaun Stribling are dealing with injuries, and Christian Kirk is sidelined with a calf injury. Jordan Watkins and Jacob Cowing are nothing more than question marks, leaving Demarcus Robinson as a virtual lock to make the roster as a veteran presence. The team was forced to add KhaDarel Hodge to the room as insurance to run one-on-ones in training camp. Samuel’s contract details are a signal for his usage. The 49ers are looking for 800 total yards, while using Samuel in a myriad of positions on the field. Running back, wide receiver, decoy, and kick returner are some of his tasks in 2026. 49ers GM John Lynch outlined the plans for Samuel on special teams. “The dynamic kickoff has brought the kickoff return back to the game,” Lynch said. “You’ve got to be really well positioned. … He’s committed to kind of doing that. … We look forward to using him there. But then offensively, you guys have seen him, and I think Kyle has a great vision in being real creative in how we use him.” Samuel has stepped back in the building and hasn’t missed a beat. The wide receiver spoke to ESPN’s Nick Wagoner about his return and how the one-year deal came together. “It kind of felt like I didn’t even go nowhere, to be honest,” Samuel said, via ESPN . “When I got back, I was just like, ‘Well, I know what’s going on. I know the people here. Staff still the same.’ So it’s kind of like the same for real.” “Conversations with me, John and Kyle have just always kind of been the same,” Samuel said. “It was just a matter of time before it happened.” Samuel spoke about leaving for Washington via trade and reiterated there was zero animosity towards Lynch and 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan. It sounds like even without the injuries to the 49ers receiver room, the team was interested in bringing back the wide back.
author: Jason Aponte

title: 49ers add another wide receiver to the injury list
summary: The San Francisco 49ers return to practice Wednesday after having Tuesday off. Nick Bosa, Osa Odighizuwa and Dre Greenlaw will all sit out with “general soreness.” However, four other players with new injuries will miss Wednesday’s session: OL Carver Willis (concussion)FB Kyle Juszczyk (finger)WR Jacob Cowing (hip flexor)OL Brett Toth (undisclosed) Cowing can’t afford to […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - JANUARY 05: Jacob Cowing #19 of the San Francisco 49ers runs with the ball against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium on January 05, 2025 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Norm Hall/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers return to practice Wednesday after having Tuesday off. Nick Bosa, Osa Odighizuwa and Dre Greenlaw will all sit out with “general soreness.” However, four other players with new injuries will miss Wednesday’s session: OL Carver Willis (concussion) FB Kyle Juszczyk (finger) WR Jacob Cowing (hip flexor) OL Brett Toth (undisclosed) Cowing can’t afford to miss any practice time, as other young receivers like Junior Bergen are on his heels. Plus, with his lengthy injury history, he won’t be afforded much grace, if any, when it comes down to final cuts. The 49ers are going to side with a player who isn’t consistently injured. Hip flexors are tricky, and it’s generally an injury that keeps a player out for a couple of weeks if it’s a mild strain. Wide receivers Mike Evans, De’Zhaun Stribling, and Christian Kirk are still not practicing. That leaves the door open for one of the young receivers to step in and make a name for themselves. The second-team offense has been a struggle — mainly because it’s really the 3s and 4s with all of the injuries. They take a hit with Toth and Willis sidelined. Rookie defensive tackle Gracen Halton is back after missing a few practices with a knee bone bruise.

title: Should the 49ers risk playing their starters in Week 1 of the preseason?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NCAA. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in 49ers fans and fans across the country. The San Francisco 49ers will have their first preseason game next Thursday, August 13, against the Tennessee Titans. The team will hold a joint practice with […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JANUARY 11: Ji'Ayir Brown #27 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates after an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on January 11, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NCAA. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in 49ers fans and fans across the country. The San Francisco 49ers will have their first preseason game next Thursday, August 13, against the Tennessee Titans. The team will hold a joint practice with Robert Saleh’s squad earlier in the week. How the joint practice goes could determine how many starters play. How many healthy first-teamers there are will also factor in the decision. Today we’re asking whether the 49ers should risk playing their starters next week, and if so, for how long? Not all starters are created equally. Brock Purdy should probably play a series. Hand the ball off a couple of times, maybe throw a screen, swing pass to the running back, maybe a slant, and call it a day. On the other side of the ball, a new scheme is being introduced. We don’t need to see Fred Warner and Dre Greenlaw. But the safeties should get as many live reps as possible this month. Ji’Ayir Brown has had a strong camp. You want to see if that carries over against a different offense when the live bullets are flying. Marque Sigle will need to play regardless, but that’s even more true with Malik Mustapha sidelined with a hamstring injury . The defensive line isn’t as cut and dry, with the plethora of injuries. You want to get as many of the young guys run, but depth could be an issue. By all accounts, Romello Height looks like he’s the real deal. Let him play a couple of series and leave it at that, because that’s a player expected to play a significant role during the regular season. full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JULY 31: Philadelphia Eagles linebacker Joshua Uche (13) participates in a drill with linebacker Ogbo Okoronkwo (50) during training camp on July 31, 2025 at the Novacare Complex in Philadelphia, PA (Photo by John Jones/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers worked out Ogbo Okoronkwo this past Sunday. On Wednesday morning, the team officially reunited Okoronkwo with Raheem Morris. The former fifth-round pick out of the 2018 NFL Draft has played with some of the best defensive coordinators in the NFL, including Morris, DeMeco Ryans, Jim Schwartz, and Vic Fangio. Okoronkwo, 31, has been a backup for most of his career. He played sparingly under Morris in the one year they spent together with the Rams. Okoronkwo actually played more in Los Angeles once Morris left. From the 2022 to 2024 seasons, he played around 400 snaps per season. To date, Okoronkwo’s best year came with the Texans in 2022, where he generated a 18.5% pressure rate, had 33 stops, and 5 sacks. The 49ers are in need of edge rush help after losing a potential depth piece in Mikail Kamara to a torn ACL , Keion White with an adductor injury , and Cameron Sample to a knee injury. Mykel Williams remains on the active/PUP List, while Nick Bosa continues to work his way up to participating in 11-on-11 drills. The injuries had mounted to a point where rookie Jaden Dugger was working with the pass rushers . Dugger might continue to cross-train there, but Okoronkwo at least gives that room a veteran who knows what is being asked of Morris’s scheme.

Asked about Evans’ absence by CBS Sports , Egbuka described the franchise legend as being “Tampa through and through,” noting that Evans has become virtually synonymous with the Buccaneers. Evans spent 12 seasons in Tampa Bay before beginning a new chapter with the San Francisco 49ers this offseason. View this post on Instagram For Egbuka, however, Evans’ impact extends far beyond his production on the field. The second-year receiver expressed gratitude for the opportunity to spend his rookie season learning directly from one of the most accomplished players in franchise history. “I am just really grateful that I got to spend a year with him,” Egbuka said, adding that he expects Evans to accomplish great things in San Francisco. Now, both sides have moved forward. Evans has begun his next chapter with the 49ers, while Egbuka and Tampa Bay’s reshaped receiving corps prepare to establish a new identity without the franchise’s longtime cornerstone.

title: Cam Ward 2026 passing yards: What’s a success for Titans QB?
summary: Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward is expected to take a sizable step forward as a sophomore. After an impressive rookie season despite lackluster surroundings, the Titans bet big on Ward this offseason. They invested in his development by hiring Brian Daboll as his OC, and adding Wan’Dale Robinson and Carnell Tate at wide receiver. Ward […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Nashville, TN, USA; Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward (1) talks with the media post practice during day 1 of mini-camp at Vanderbilt Health Football Center. Mandatory Credit: Steve Roberts-Imagn Images | Steve Roberts-Imagn Images Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward is expected to take a sizable step forward as a sophomore. After an impressive rookie season despite lackluster surroundings, the Titans bet big on Ward this offseason. They invested in his development by hiring Brian Daboll as his OC, and adding Wan’Dale Robinson and Carnell Tate at wide receiver. Ward finished his rookie season with 3,169 passing yards, 15 touchdowns, and seven interceptions. Ward had two head coaches (Brian Callahan and Mike McCoy) and two play callers (Callahan and Mike McCoy). His top wide receivers were fourth-round rookies Chimere Dike and Elic Ayomanor. Ward finished his rookie season ranked 17th in passing yards. The No. 1 overall pick likely would have been 16th had he not injured his shoulder on the first series of the Week 18 regular season finale. With a massive sophomore campaign looming, how many passing yards would you consider a success for Ward in 2026? The theme of OTAs and minicamp was that Ward apparently struggled . He’s learning Daboll’s offense while figuring out how to test tight throwing windows. Ward was better at minicamp than OTAs, proving he’s growing in Daboll’s scheme. We’re now underway at training camp, where he’s had mostly positive practices to date. Ward should aim for about 3,500 passing yards in 2026. That total would have placed 13th in the league last season ahead of Jordan Love and Aaron Rodgers. If Ward starts all 17 games, he’d just need to average roughly 206 passing yards per game to reach 3,500. Titans fans are hoping Ward takes a Drake Maye or Caleb Williams-like sophomore step. Maye finished fourth in passing yards last season with 4,394. Williams was seventh with 3,942. Perhaps Ward can flirt with 4,000 passing yards if he really thrives in Daboll’s system. Expectations are high for Ward as a sophomore. About 3,500+ passing yards would signal a success. Hopefully Ward establishes himself as the Titans’ franchise quarterback in 2026.

title: Analyzing storylines from first set of Commanders padded practices
summary: The addition of Stefon Diggs on Wednesday is the big news of the week, but there are still plenty of other Commanders storylines to cover. Washington players were in pads for the first time Monday, and the team responded with their best practice of camp thus far. The players went without pads on Tuesday before […]
full_text: The addition of Stefon Diggs on Wednesday is the big news of the week , but there are still plenty of other Commanders storylines to cover. Washington players were in pads for the first time Monday, and the team responded with their best practice of camp thus far. The players went without pads on Tuesday before suiting up again on a rainy Wednesday . There was a lot to cover in those three days. Key Commanders players look sharp early The 2025 season did not go according to plan for many of the Washington Commanders’ star players. Quarterback Jayden Daniels battled injuries and inconsistent play, receiver Terry McLaurin sat out a good portion of training camp while missing time in the regular season due to injury, and future Hall of Famer Bobby Wagner’s play fell off substantially. Monday’s practice was a big step towards putting last year’s disappointing season behind them and moving forward with a new attitude and energy. Daniels started the week sharp, throwing a dot to tight end Chig Okonkwo in the back of the end zone and following it up with a pinpoint fade to McLaurin. Daniels looked in control of the new offense, and before Monday’s practice, Dan Quinn said he is “ further ahead ” with the new scheme than Quinn imagined he would be at this point. Daniels stayed hot on Tuesday, slinging the ball with a quick release, and looked sharp all three days. TERRY MCLAURIN AND 1 😱 via @BleedinBnG pic.twitter.com/LN7a14t7BO — Outta Pocket with RGIII (@OuttaPocketRG3) August 3, 2026 Today is by far the best the offense has looked. Specifically Jayden. He’s processing and delivering really well #RaiseHail — Denton Day (D-Day) (@TheDentonDay) August 5, 2026 McLaurin did his part, hauling in the throw on the corner and looking like his old self. Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles also met early first-round expectations when the pads came on Monday and made a splash play of his own to start the first padded practice. He also had another to finish the session Wednesday. Just sipping coffee and watching Sonny Styles be a grown ass man This dude is going to be a stud pic.twitter.com/bqrihq31wp — Will Compton (@_willcompton) August 4, 2026 Sonny Styles closed practice with a big pop on Jacory Croskey-Merritt in a goal-line drill. Was hard to see from our vantage point so saw Jeremy Reaves in the scrum and celebrating so wondered if he made the pop. “No, that was all Sonny,” he said. — John Keim (@john_keim) August 5, 2026 Sam Cosmi was bringing it on Monday as well, driving defenders off the ball, he followed it with a rest day on Tuesday before returning Wednesday. Everyone expects these names to play well, but it is always a welcome sight for key players to perform at a high level. Many have noted that Daniels looks sharper in camp this year than the last two. How will the linebacker room shake out this season? One of the big talking points last week was the confirmation of Leo Chenal and Sonny Styles possibly playing in dual MIKE roles this season, but Frankie Luvu stepped into the linebacker conversation this week. The team started full field work, and the defense utilized some 4-3 looks with Styles as the MIKE, Luvu at WILL, and Leo on the ball as a strong side backer. So far, Luvu is having a good camp and looks like his old self in the new scheme. Frankie Luvu looks like a completely different guy… visually and physically.. he’s flying around like it’s 2024 — Bleeding Burgundy & Gold (@BleedinBnG) August 3, 2026 Of note, Luvu also appeared to be wearing the green dot during Tuesday’s session. Linebacker utilization is one of the items the team wants to keep under wraps, and while Frankie might not match his snap total from last season, coordinator Daronte Jones appears poised to use Luvu as a blitzer and disruptor where he could be more effective in less snaps. Fight is on for the last roster spot in the wide-receiver room The Diggs addition clearly changes the roster math for the wide receivers. While there has been some speculation the team could keep seven wide receivers, there will be a roster crunch for a team that plans to utilize heavy personnel groupings. McLaurin, Diggs, and Williams are all locks, and Luke McCaffrey made his case to be one this week. He had a good day of practice on Monday and a great one on Tuesday with multiple receptions and a catch-and-run for a long touchdown. He followed it up with another splash play on Wednesday. a Luke touchdown for you 🫵 @mccaffrey_luke | #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/tAIu8LcFeQ — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 4, 2026 Luke McCaffrey is having another good day. Just had a nice touchdown in the back of the endzone from Jayden on an over route. Got both feet down too. #Commanders — Josh Taylor (@JoshTaylorFB) August 5, 2026 It’s all about stacking good days on top of each other in camp, and McCaffrey has been the best at it so far. Dyami Brown and Jaylin Lane both had drops on key throws and need to build more consistency, but Lane should make the roster as a punt returner. Daniels singled out Treylon Burks in his wide receiver discussion on Saturday, and after recovering from foot soreness, Burks continued to take first-team reps alongside McCaffery. Van Jefferson has also looked good at times. The last wide receiver will need to be a contributor on special teams, which still gives undrafted free agent Jaden Bradley a chance at a roster spot. In Week 6 of his senior season at UNLV, Bradley blocked a punt and also returned a different blocked punt for a touchdown. Bradley also returned five kickoffs for 106 yards and one punt for 36 yards over the course of the season. When will the Commanders injured players return? Ahkello Witherspoon was placed on the reserve/retired list on Tuesday. While the team added Fabian Moreau as a reasonable depth piece, the loss of another player in the cornerback room highlighted the need to get Trey Amos back on the field. The second-year cornerback was sighted at camp this week, in good spirits and moving well, and the team will reassess his availability today. Tress Way was seen getting some punts in before practice on Wednesday and will also be evaluated at the same time. The team added a center in Trey Hill , but it was more for practice functionality than concern over Allegretti’s injury. Still, Washington needs to get Nick back sooner than later. Julian Good-Jones had another bad snap during Tuesday’s session while Matt Gulbin continues to be brought along slowly . The team also seems to have focused on developing Tim McKay at center so he can bring his versatility at all three positions along the offensive line. Guard Timothy McKay (his full name always trips me up with that other guy) is taking snaps with that group — Martenzie Johnson (@10zJohnson) August 5, 2026 As expected, there is still no timeline for Dorance Armstrong and Deatrich Wise , and it was reported earlier that tight end John Bates would be out for at least another week. The team did get linebacker Kain Medrano back on Monday, and he immediately made his presence known with an interception . Several players also missed Wednesday’s session, so we will wait for an update there. #Commanders on the active roster I don't see at practice today: – RB Jeremy McNichols (undisclosed) – C Nick Allegretti (calf) – TE John Bates (hamstring) – OLB K'Lavon Chaisson (undisclosed) – DE Drake Jackson (illness) – CB Amik Robertson (undisclosed) — Tashan Reed (@tashanreed) August 5, 2026 UDFA Watch The kicking matchup between Jake Moody and Drew Stevens looked fairly even on Monday, but Stevens pulled ahead in Tuesday’s session, going 5-for-5, including a 55-yarder with plenty of room to spare. Moody went 3-for-5, missing two field goals in the kicking session and another in the team’s 11-on-11 sessions. There is a long way to go in the competition, but right now the UDFA has the edge. full_text: The Daily Slop – August 6, 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. But… have to make sure today. pic.twitter.com/eZPnAhGg1z — John Keim (@john_keim) August 6, 2026 Articles JP Finlay Stefon Diggs’ signing proves Adam Peters learned a lesson [I]n multiple conversations with sources close to the Patriots locker room – Diggs was a model citizen and leader for the young players last year. So now he’s coming to Washington. Coming home. A product of Good Counsel High School and the University of Maryland is now wearing burgundy and gold. Diggs makes the Commanders a better football team. Immediately. Breaking news on Inside Training Camp Live: Stefon Diggs is signing with the #Commanders . pic.twitter.com/gtzLxXDFCc — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) August 5, 2026 He has elite hands and runs great routes. He will be invaluable to Daniels on 3rd downs and in the red zone. Last year he was still recovering from a major knee injury suffered in 2024. This year, it’s entirely possible Diggs gets more speed back to add to his veteran savvy. The Commanders defense was awful in 2025 so Peters set out to fix it. He spent real money on the defensive line, used his 1st-round pick on LB Sonny Styles, and invested in the defensive backs. The defense already looks different, faster and possibly much better. On offense, however, questions remained at receiver. Now there’s far fewer questions. The expectation from the team is that Stefon Diggs will most likely have his first press conference after Friday's practice. — Scott Abraham (@Scott7news) August 5, 2026 It would be tremendous if somebody from the collection of Treylon Burks, Luke McCaffrey, Dyami Brown, Jaylen Lane or rookie Antonio Williams breaks out for a great year. But that happening is hardly a given, and now there’s much less of a need for that to happen. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE NOTUS The former Patriot is expected to slot in as Washington’s No. 2 receiver, answering one of the offseason’s biggest questions A source close to Diggs said the 32-year-old DMV native chose Washington because he was impressed by the entire organization, from the front office to the coaches to the players. Diggs, a four-time Pro Bowler, wanted a “chance to play with one of best young [quarterbacks] and opposite one of [the] best receivers — and to do it all at home,” the source said. His 9,032 receiving yards since 2018 is the third-most in that time period behind only Davante Adams (9,822) and Tyreek Hill (9,587). Putting a player with 942 career receptions, 11,504 yards and 74 touchdowns alongside Terry McLaurin (498 receptions, 6,961 yards and 41 touchdowns) makes the receiving unit deep and dangerous. The two veterans will be grouped with promising rookie Antonio Williams, who has had breakout moments during training camp. Diggs has also garnered headlines away from the field. In May, he was found not guilty of assaulting his private chef. He is currently suing a social media influencer who has accused him of sexual assault and facing a civil lawsuit for accusing a former concierge of stealing his Ferrari. The conversation has gone from "who is the Commanders' WR-2?" to "can they keep a 7th WR so that Dyami Brown or Van Jefferson hangs around?" This move completely changes the room and the feeling about the talent around Daniels in a huge season. — Grant Paulsen (@GrantPaulsen) August 5, 2026 To read more of this article, CLICK HERE ESPN Will WR Stefon Diggs be a fit with the Washington Commanders? Why Diggs and not other WR options? It was either Diggs or bust for Washington — nobody used those words, but one team source said he was the only free agent they were interested in signing at this time. Washington lost out on other possibilities in the offseason. It had wanted to sign Alec Pierce, but he opted to re-sign with Indianapolis before free agency; one league source said Pierce would have signed with the Commanders — had he come free. They also tried, but failed, to sign Romeo Doubs. And Carnell Tate would have been an option had he been available with the seventh pick. In other words, they had kept searching for more at the position. Why did the Commanders wait so long to sign him? And does his delayed start hurt his chances to make an early impact? There were multiple reasons. At one point, Brandon Aiyuk appeared to be a possibility — Washington was just waiting for him to be released from the 49ers. The Commanders would have been interested, according to multiple team sources. But he has yet to be cut. So that likelihood diminished this summer, putting them more on a path to Diggs, who was always going to be the more expensive option. Also, with Diggs not in camp, others — notably rookie Williams — have gotten more reps — and a better chance for Washington to see what it had in its receiving corps. Williams in particular will play a key role, and there are similarities in how he’d be used along with Diggs. It’s also possible that Diggs wanted to see what other opportunities arose — or the money just wasn’t right. But he had made it known that he would like to play in Washington. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) What WR Stefon Diggs brings to the Washington Commanders So what does Diggs bring to Washington? In a word; production. He’s had over 1000 receiving yards in seven of his last eight seasons. The only time he didn’t break 1000 yards during that eight year span was in 2024, where he tore his ACL after eight games, but even then he was on target to hit 1000 yards. Last year he bounced back from that ACL and had another 1000 yard season with the Patriots, becoming their top receiver on their way to the Super Bowl. But what makes him so productive and can he continue to be that productive at age 32? Let’s take a closer look. One of the first things that stood out to me when watching Diggs film from last year wasn’t the route running or the catching ability. I’ll certainly get to those things in this post, but the thing that jumped out to me most was his ability to make himself available. Diggs consistently showed the awareness to know when his route was dead and how to adjust or go off-script to make himself available. It’s a veteran savviness that made Zach Ertz such a great target for Jayden Daniels the past two years. Diggs does this consistently on film. Sometimes it’s making small adjustments like sitting a route down in a hole in coverage, sometimes it’s going off-script when a play breaks down to make himself available. He’s been around multiple teams and multiple quarterbacks and always managed to build up a rapport with them quickly, likely due to this ability. It means when things break down and the quarterback is in trouble, they typically look to him to bail them out of it. An outside WR much of his career, the former University of Maryland standout split time on the perimeter and in the slot with the Patriots. Washington has slot options in rookie Antonio Williams, Luke McCaffrey and Jaylin Lane. It’s…

title: Washington Commanders Week 2 training camp observations, standouts
summary: There is a lot going on in Ashburn, VA, as the Commanders are now over a full week into training camp. Unlike previous camps run by head coach Dan Quinn, this one seems a lot different in everything from access to vet rest days. What has been an entertaining start is expected to ramp up […]
full_text: There is a lot going on in Ashburn, VA, as the Commanders are now over a full week into training camp. Unlike previous camps run by head coach Dan Quinn , this one seems a lot different in everything from access to vet rest days. What has been an entertaining start is expected to ramp up even more as we head towards joint practices next week against the Dolphins. That’s especially true after Wednesday afternoon’s once-year pact with receiver Stefon Diggs . Before we look forward to all that on a Thursday off date on the training-camp calendar, let’s look back at my observations as we get into Week 2. Who has been running with the first team? Camp is a time to mix things up and see what guys can do when they are in certain situations. There is certainly a LOT of rotation going on, but from a first-team glance, this appears to be the way things have played out very early in camp, though the receiver should change with Diggs coming aboard. Offense: QB: Jayden Daniels RB: Bill Croskey-Merritt WR: Terry McLaurin WR: Treylon Burks WR: Luke McCaffrey TE: Chig Okonkwo TE 2 (12 personnel): Ben Sinnott LT: Laremy Tunsil LG: Chris Paul C: Julian Good-Jones (while Nick Allegretti has been out) RG: Sam Cosmi RT: Josh Conerly *Antonio Williams and Brandon Coleman have also gotten some work with the first team. Defense: EDGE: Odafe Oweh DT: Daron Payne DT: Javon Kinlaw DT 3 (when in an odd front): Tim Settle EDGE: K’Lavon Chaisson ILB: Frankie Luvu ILB: Sonny Styles SAM (walked-up): Leo Chenal CB: Mike Sainristil CB: Amik Robertson S: Nick Cross S: Jeremy Reaves S: Will Harris *Sainristil has been seeing time on the outside and in the slot. Before his abrupt retirement, Witherspoon was the other outside corner when Mikey was in the slot, with Rasul Douglas seeing some time mixed in with the first team on the outside. The Green Dot There was talk that rookie Sonny Styles or free agent signing Leo Chenal would get the green dot for defensive communication. After a week of camp, however, it appears Frankie Luvu is directing the defense. As The Athletic reporter Nicki Jhabvala says below, it’s still early and things can change once live action is upon us in September, but as of now, this is where things stand. For the “green dot” crowd … it’s still early, but Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw have both said that Frankie Luvu has been that guy getting everyone set. — Nicki Jhabvala (@NickiJhabvala) August 4, 2026 Camp standouts: Luke McCaffrey: The third-year wideout continues to stack good practices. He was a beast on Tuesday , having arguably the best practice of all the Commanders, and scored again Wednesday in team work on a dime from quarterback Jayden. He’s working both inside and outside and has been said to look good wherever he’s lining up. Ben Sinnott: The increased playing time is certainly benefitting Sinnott. He’s working with the ones in 12 personnel and coordinator David Blough is using him in a variety of different ways, including in-line and as an H-back. Bill Croskey-Merritt: Bill is noticeably bigger and is bringing that physicality with him during runs, however, it’s his hands out of the backfield that have stood out early on. Odafe Oweh/K’Lavon Chaisson: The EDGE duo have been as advertised, and MORE! Camp observers have spoken of the explosion to which both players get off the ball and there have been plays every day where the whistle needs to be blown to protect the quarterbacks. Sonny Styles: The way he triggers is just different! He’s a true sideline-to-sideline defender who brought the wood a few times during padded practice . Teammates have raved about his preparation, fluidity and overall athleticism. Frankie Luvu: Observers have stated that Luvu looks like the 2024 version, not the one we saw struggle last season. He’s been looking great on timely blitzes. Sam Cosmi: Fully healthy now, Cosmi is said to be bullying guys out there, especially during Monday’s padded practice one-on-one session. Nick Cross: Cross has been all over the field, and there were many times when observers said if it was live action, he would have blown the play up. He’s going to have a big role for this new defense. Colson Yankoff: Yankoff, who has seen more time with the first and second groups with John Bates out, has made the most of his opportunities. That’s especially true in the passing game; hauling in a few really impressive catches in traffic. Josh Josephs: The rookie has impressed with his length, get-off and even coverage ability working primarily with the second group. Antonio Williams: Observers have commented on how smooth Williams is and how quickly he can uncover. He’s been with the second group a lot and backup quarterback Marcus Mariota has missed him on a few occasions where he’s been wide open. On Wednesday, during the second padded practice, he absolutely TOASTED the third- and fourth-string defense for an easy touchdown. Rasul Douglas: Douglas showed up the first two days of camp, when observers said he was all around the ball. He had a pick-six on Day 2 and supposedly looked pretty good during padded practice. Mike Sainristil: It’s been a mixed bag for Sainristil in coverage, but observers have said he’s constantly working, and it seems when he gets beat, he comes back and makes some plays. His leadership has been lauded by some of the coaches. Jeremy Reaves: Coaches have praised his effort and communication in this new defense. Who has struggled? There is a lot of praise early in camp, so the observations on who has struggled have been limited. Below is some of what I have heard early on. Marcus Mariota: Observers have said he’s not seeing things as quickly and hasn’t pulled the trigger on some throws he should have made. Quan Martin: Martin has been running with the second team after being a starter the previous two seasons. I’m not hearing that he’s been particularly bad, but he may have lost his starting job early on. He did get stiff-armed into another galaxy today by Fatman Allen. Jaylin Lane: Lane had some early drop issues, but it seems he has cleared those up over the past few sessions. Consistency will be key for the second-year pro. Car’lin Vigers: The young corner made some plays during the first day of camp, but recent reports are that he’s struggled staying with receivers in his zone. Josh Conerly: I don’t know how much struggling Conerly has actually done considering Washington has been in pads just two days, but MANY reports out of practice cite both Oweh and Chaisson getting into the backfield quickly, and I don’t believe Tunsil’s name was mentioned as someone who has been blowing a lot of pass sets. Competition between Blough and Jones We knew this would be a theme all camp, but it’s so refreshing to hear that coordinators David Blough and Daronte Jones are out here playing 3D chess against one another during sessions. Iron shapes iron, so this is absolutely music to my ears, especially after putting up with two very predictable offenses and defenses over the past two seasons. Blough has also been getting into his bag of tricks, as he looks for ways to slow down Jones’ furious rush. Wednesday he had, by all accounts, three trick plays, including a pretty hook-and-ladder between Jayden, Terry and Burks.
author: Mark Tyler

title: State of Commanders receiver corps after Stefon Diggs acquisition
summary: The Commanders receiver corps obviously got better with the Stefon Diggs acquisition. The veteran is a top-tier route runner and a steady producer with a long track record of success. While he’s 32 years old, Diggs can still move and make important catches in the clutch.   Head coach Dan Quinn has established a competitive […]
full_text: The Commanders receiver corps obviously got better with the Stefon Diggs acquisition . The veteran is a top-tier route runner and a steady producer with a long track record of success. While he’s 32 years old, Diggs can still move and make important catches in the clutch. Head coach Dan Quinn has established a competitive Commanders training camp, but it’s safe to say Diggs will eventually step into the No. 2 receiver slot opposite Terry McLaurin. He’s expected to get significant playing time and get targeted a ton, even though he may not be a true every-down player after playing 55% of the offensive snaps in New England last season. He’ll also impact his position group just by joining it. A roster spot just got harder to earn at the position with Terry McLaurin, Diggs and third-round pick Antonio Williams as roster locks. Jaylin Lane’s punt-return ability makes him darn-close to one, with maybe two more roster spots available. Fierce battles will be waged for those, among talented individuals. A few thoughts on how the Diggs addition might impact the receiver corps. Terry McLaurin Terry will remain scary while continuing to move around the formation as new coordinator David Blough always intended. McLaurin is the alpha around here, on a long-term deal and one of the longest-tenured players on the Commanders roster. He also has an even-keeled leadership vibe that will hold his position group together and help it improve with all the extra behind-the-scenes work he does. None of that will change with Diggs around. The new guy commands respect and should keep defenses from focusing too heavily on McLaurin. That’s nothing but a positive for the veteran, who could be in for a monster year. Antonio Williams Having a savvy veteran who’s next-level at creating separation should help the young rookie become more adept in his own right at creating separation. It should actually be a huge help in his development. Toss out those thoughts of Diggs impeding Williams’ progress. This will allow the third-round pick to develop without the pressure of having to be a primary target early in his first professional season. Trust me, if Williams gets open a ton and builds trust, quarterback Jayden Daniels will throw him the football. While Williams has experience and college production playing in the slot, he could move around a bunch like Diggs and McLaurin. Jaylin Lane/Luke McCaffrey These young guys have speed and have flashed potential as NFL playmakers. Both guys can take the top off a defense and at least expand a coverage area to create room for others. Development will be key for both players this summer, as they work to earn opportunities and provide the quality depth most good teams possess. Injuries happen, and the Commanders must be ready for them. Treylon Burks The Diggs signing might’ve impacted the fifth-year veteran the most. Treylon Burks was in the conversation to be Washington’s No. 2 receiver, with a shot to be a heavily-involved on-field presence. That seems unlikely now, if the top receivers stay healthy. Burks still has a lot to offer in terms of size and physicality in the pattern, but a large sum of targets potentially available to him might be gone now. He can earn a role on the team with a solid summer, but he has more of an uphill battle to that end than he did on Tuesday. Dyami Brown Head coach Dan Quinn was complimentary of Brown on Wednesday morning, saying how much better he looks in this second stint in Washington. He has solid chemistry with Daniels , which puts him in serious play for a roster spot. Realistic expectations around his involvement certainly dropped on Wednesday, though. Everything we just discussed is projection, though, with much of training camp and the preseason to sort things out now that Diggs is a Commander. A way-too-early WR roster projection: Terry McLaurin Stefon Diggs Antonio Williams Jaylin Lane Luke McCaffrey Treylon Burks *NOTE: I have a tough time seeing seven receivers make the 53-man roster, even with two returners in the position group. There are too many other depth needs in other spots. I also think Burks could make it over Dyami Brown because he’s a big dude and his physical, contested-catch ability could be useful within this group, but it’s a toss-up. Lane and McCaffrey provide speed. Burks and Brown will battle it out, forcing coaches to make a tough decision on the sixth receiver. What do you think of this receiver roster projection? Who’s impacted most by the Diggs signing? Who’s helped by it? Let everyone know in the comments below.
author: Scott Bair

title: How Stefon Diggs will help Jayden Daniels, elevate Commanders offense
summary: The Commanders need an established, legit No. 2 receiver opposite Terry McLaurin to help quarterback Jayden Daniels.   That statement was true back in 2024. And in 2025. And again, heading into 2026 training camp.   It isn’t a fact anymore. Not after the Commanders agreed on terms of a one-year contract with veteran receiver […]
full_text: The Commanders need an established, legit No. 2 receiver opposite Terry McLaurin to help quarterback Jayden Daniels. That statement was true back in 2024. And in 2025. And again, heading into 2026 training camp. It isn’t a fact anymore. Not after the Commanders agreed on terms of a one-year contract with veteran receiver Stefon Diggs. A league source confirmed the pact on Wednesday afternoon, which ESPN reports is worth up to $12 million . Commanders general manager Adam Peters fortified the team’s greatest roster weakness with the Diggs addition, adding an established producer to a position group previously lacking it outside of McLaurin. Diggs is a tide to lift all boats, someone who will make those around him better. He’ll take coverage away from McLaurin and tight end Chig Okonkwo. He’ll allow rookie third-round pick Antonio Williams to develop without the pressure of needing to make a massive and immediate impact. He’ll be a leader by example in terms of route running and creating separation for all pass catchers and Williams in particular. I mean, just look at these highlights: Welcome home to Stefon Diggs. "We all we got, we all we need." The floor has been elevated. #RaiseHail #Terps pic.twitter.com/BBVODzZjBu — George Carmi (@Gcarmi21) August 5, 2026 Diggs is also a quarterback-friendly receiver who will do wonders for Jayden Daniels. While he hasn’t averaged above 12 yards per reception since 2022, Diggs remains steadily productive. That’s what Daniels needs, maybe above all else. Diggs has exceeded 1,000 receiving yards in seven of his last eight seasons , save a 2024 campaign in Houston where he tore an ACL. Diggs rebounded from that event in a big way, totaling 85 catches for 1,103 receiving yards and three touchdowns on 105 targets in his first (and only) season with the New England Patriots. Going deeper inside those numbers shows immense value and the reliability Daniels needs, as expressed with stats unearthed by Warren Sharp. Stefon Diggs to DC his 2025 season: #1 EPA/target (+0.68) #2 success rate (66%) #6 yards/target (9.9) the consistency was MASSIVE: #1 catch rate (83%) #1 accurate target catch rate (89%) #1 lowest WR error rate (2%) and only 2 drops all season! (out of all WR w 100+ targ) pic.twitter.com/gLJWDSM8PE — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) August 5, 2026 That’s trust quantified right there. Diggs will make the quarterback better, and he’ll make skill players around him better because he’s a threat who has earned opponent’s respect. He’s also become known as a vocal leader later in his career with high standards (and maybe some tough love) and expectations for those around him. His resume should command respect, though it will still remain McLaurin’s meeting room. He’s the alpha in Washington, even with Diggs around. It’s also important that Diggs sign at this point in camp, with sufficient time to learn David Blough’s new offense and its verbiage. There’s alaso time to get reps with Daniels and to bond with the Commanders other pass catchers. Diggs doesn’t come to Washington as a savior. He is a high-efficacy supplement to a Commanders roster with tremendous upside and a top-tier quarterback who comes through in the clutch. He’s 32 years old, but the DMV native and University of Maryland product remains in great shape and seems genuinely excited to play near his hometown. Stefon Diggs is at Maryland’s first fall practice. “Shout out to my Terps, man. And go Commanders. Let’s go.” pic.twitter.com/QIghaTF2a2 — Scott Bair (@ScottBairNFL) August 5, 2026 Mark Tyler and John Portis will surely chime in with more detailed breakdowns of Diggs’ fit in the coming days, but it doesn’t take a film expert to realize how the veteran receiver can help Daniels and a Washington offense that could’ve been good without him. Now that Diggs is in the mix, it should be much, much better. How does the Stefon Diggs signing change your expectations for the Commanders offense in 2026? Let us know in the comments below:

title: What we’ve learned from the Commanders’ first week of training camp
summary: We’re just one week into training camp, and the Washington Commanders are already beginning to answer many of the biggest questions that surrounded their roster entering the 2026 season. Offensively, Washington entered camp confident its wide receiver and center depth could withstand the difficulties of a 17-game season. That confidence is already being tested, however, […]
full_text: We’re just one week into training camp, and the Washington Commanders are already beginning to answer many of the biggest questions that surrounded their roster entering the 2026 season. Offensively, Washington entered camp confident its wide receiver and center depth could withstand the difficulties of a 17-game season. That confidence is already being tested, however, as projected starting center Nick Allegretti (calf) is missing valuable practice time with an early camp injury . Practices under new offensive coordinator David Blough have seemingly breathed life into the team’s tight ends, and while injuries have created uncertainty up front, they’ve also opened opportunities elsewhere. John Bates is missing time due to an injury, though Ben Sinnott and Colson Yankoff each have had shining moments throughout the first few practices. With Sinnott and Yankoff both stepping up to the plate, the real question now centers on which guy proves themselves more valuable to Blough? Sinnott, a former second-round pick, is finally receiving meaningful opportunities. Instead of running away with the job, he’s locked in a legitimate competition with Colson Yankoff for a larger role in Blough’s offense. Defensively, one of the biggest offseason questions centered on new coordinator Daronte Jones and what his defense would look like once practices began. Jones has quickly established an aggressive, attacking defensive identity, and his players are loving it. Odafe Oweh , Javon Kinlaw , Jeremy Reaves and Daron Payne are some who all shared great perspective on his teaching style and scheme. Jones has frequently moved the front seven into multiple alignments, creating unpredictability and forcing the offense to identify pressure and assignments differently on nearly every snap. A major question headed into training camp was the depth of the cornerback room. Rasul Douglas was a signing at the start of camp and has quickly made his presence felt early with turnovers and pass breakups. Trey Amos, as of today, is still recovering from last season’s leg injury, and he’s scheduled to be reassessed on Thursday. Ahkello Witherspoon was placed on Washington’s reserve/retired list, prompting Washington to sign Fabian Moreau . Whether the group can hold up over a 17-game season remains unanswered, but ,Washington, to me, has at least turned what looked like a glaring weakness into a position that appears capable of competing. On the latest Trap or Dive Podcast , Dre and I dive into the Training Camp Chronicles of the Washington Commanders, discussing our major takeaways from the first week of practices. Specifically, we discuss: Washington’s issue at Center Ben Sinnott vs. Colson Yankoff Cornerback room; Rasul Douglas impact Running back room is shining Ideal nickel defense Podcast: YouTube : Comment and let us know your thoughts a week into Washington’s training camp, and subscribe to the Trap or Dive Podcast.

title: Jeremy Reaves pushing hard for defensive role in Commanders camp
summary: Commanders defensive back/core special teammer Jeremy Reaves came up twice during Dan Quinn’s Tuesday morning press conference. The head coach used both questions to laud the veteran’s presence in this 2026 training camp, going well beyond the typical platitudes common this time of year.   It’s clear that Reaves has made a positive impression early […]
full_text: Commanders defensive back/core special teammer Jeremy Reaves came up twice during Dan Quinn’s Tuesday morning press conference. The head coach used both questions to laud the veteran’s presence in this 2026 training camp, going well beyond the typical platitudes common this time of year. It’s clear that Reaves has made a positive impression early on and is challenging for an increased role in Daronte Jones’ defens e. Reaves has built a career on excellent special teams play, with Pro-Bowl and All-Pro selection s honoring those efforts. His defensive contributions have been more minimal. They were virtually non-existent in 2023 – he played just five games that year – and again in 2024. His role increased in 2025, as the career safety got more involved. An injury to Will Harris created some opportunity – so did Quan Martin’s ineffectiveness — but Quinn also found ways to get him involved. Reaves posted a career-high 91 total tackles and had an interception and two passes defensed. Reaves has always been a valued presence in the Commanders locker room but he’s apparently pressing for even more in 2026. “His communication skills are elite as a ball player, as a teammate on the field and off,” Quinn said his Wednesday presser. “So much of what we’re doing goes through out communication hub at linebacker and safety, so seeing him and Frankie (Luvu) and others…he’s an initiator of so many good things that we talk through. He sets incredible standards for effort and speed. “We could use a hell of a lot more Jeremy Reaves. He’s a remarkable teammate, player – he’s definitely making his presence felt on defense more so than he has in the previous two years.” Jones is installing a new defensive system that requires different player strengths and an opportunity for everyone to compete for playing. While he may not be the most athletic player, his football IQ is sky high and he’s a physical player in the back. We’re also expecting some three-safety sets from Jones this season, so Reaves could find a role somewhere in one or more of the personnel packages. Reaves is getting a shot to prove himself in this camp. We’ll see what he makes of it. “He has earned the right to have these reps,” Quinn said. “He’s got high standards about how he wants to go. He’s very much in the mix from a defensive standpoint. As you’re starting a new, system, everyone’s on the same level to say, ‘where’s he gonna go?’ To see him take advantage of that, that’s a big deal. He has always had unique leadership communication qualities, so it’s nice to see that coming out on the defensive side as well.” What would it take for Jeremy Reaves secure significant snaps on the Commanders defense? Let us know in the comments below:

title: How Rachaad White, Jayden Daniels college connection can help Commanders
summary: Running back Rachaad White has known quarterback Jayden Daniels a long time, way before Commanders fans keyed on him prior to the 2024 NFL draft. The relationship began before his two LSU campaigns turned Daniels into a household name.   It started in 2020, after White transferred to Arizona State from a California junior college. […]
full_text: Running back Rachaad White has known quarterback Jayden Daniels a long time, way before Commanders fans keyed on him prior to the 2024 NFL draft . The relationship began before his two LSU campaigns turned Daniels into a household name. It started in 2020, after White transferred to Arizona State from a California junior college. Daniels had starred for the Sundevils a year prior, and White quickly saw something in the young signal caller. “I tell everyone this all the time. He’s just special,” White said in a press conference Wednesday after a Commanders training camp practice. “I knew that after I came into ASU, when I saw him move and throw the ball around, when I saw him in big games and how he came down in the clutch and won it for us. “To see how poised he is all the time – he just stays level-headed and even keeled. He has different things that (not everyone has). That’s what makes him unique. He has obviously matured since we were together in college but, other than that, how he handles and goes about his business, how he’s up early and how he attacks the day and always talks about football, football, football. That’s how he’s the same way (he has always been).” White has said a few time now that Daniels is the best quarterback he has ever played with. The Arizona State experience told him so, as did Daniels performance in the NFL. “He’s talented, but he can also apply himself,” White said. “I’ve seen him come through in the clutch so many times for us (at Arizona State). The same thing with his rookie year. He may have been banged up last year but, in the games he play, y’all were in those games. When you have a guy like that, and he’s so talented and the way he makes an impact, you’re going to be in every game.” Washington learned that in 2024, when Daniels was excellent in close games especially. He had four fourth-quarter comebacks and the Commanders were 8-4 in one-score games. White was starring in Tampa Bay at the time, but paid attention to Daniels’ meteoric rise. When free agency arrived and Washington showed interest, White jumped at the chance to reunite with his college teammate. The chemistry reformed quickly, picking up from a 2021 Arizona State season where both guys were awesome. Daniels has 2,380 passing yards and 10 touchdowns (and 10 picks), while White had 1,006 rushing yards and 15 rushing touchdowns, plus another 456 receiving yards. Daniels has targeted White a ton already, so the trust is already there. White is well versed on how to keep it going. “Everything with the quarterback starts with trust,” White said. “Him knowing that I know the play and I’ll be there in the right spot. He knows he can trust me to make something shake if he drops it down to me.” White’s joining a quality running back room where competition will sort out reps and roles. We discussed Bill Croskey Merritt on Tuesday, including his emphasis on improving receiving skill. White’s solid on third-down but can run inside, which makes them an enticing duo atop the depth chart. The carry/target breakdown will be influenced by this training camp and preseason, but also by matchups. Expect both guys to be heavily involved, even if neither guy sees many in-game touches. “The guys in the room (overall) do a lot of great things from the aspect of working on their game,” White said. “Bill has done a lot of things to work on his pass game and catch the ball well and working on his routes. …All of us in the room can do good things. It’s great to have everybody in there, competing against each other.” Will the chemistry between Rachaad White and Jayden Daniels lead to big receiving numbers for the running back? How will the carry split between White and Croskey-Merritt work out? Let us know in the comments below:

title: Ottis Anderson and me: A fan's quest for the meaning of the Hall of Fame
summary: One man's journey through history and psychology to make an impassioned case for his favorite Super Bowl MVP.
full_text:
I TRY NOT to feel slighted when the MVP of Super Bowl XXV doesn't hug me on a chilly December afternoon at MetLife Stadium, but it isn't easy.

 Ottis "O.J." Anderson, you see, is not stingy with hugs: former teammates, stadium buffet station chefs,  New York Giants  executives, fans too young to have seen him play, fans old enough to never forget seeing him play -- if there's reasonable justification, the 69-year-old Anderson will wrap his still oak-tree-strong arms around you.

 But not me, not yet anyway. I'm at MetLife for a game against the  Minnesota Vikings , there to hang out with Anderson. Not long after he shakes my hand upon arrival, we're sitting at a high table in the Giants Legacy Club with another retired Giant, Rodney Hampton.

 Hampton was a rookie in 1990, Anderson's 12th season in the league, and he explains that the veteran running back was asked by head coach Bill Parcells to inform him when Hampton was "ready." Taking that mandate as seriously as he did everything in his long career, Anderson mentored the player destined to replace him as a starter through a very productive campaign. "To most people that was the season he helped us win a Super Bowl," Hampton says. "But for me that was the season he taught me how to be a pro. He was everything to all of us in the [running backs] room: dad, uncle, big brother, mentor -- call him anything you want."

 Well, anything except Hall of Famer.

 

 Hampton and Anderson are sometime ambassadors for the Giants, paid to turn up at games to shmooze with fans, especially the kind who tend to watch the action from suites. Both men are naturals, quick with a selfie smile, game memory or insight about the current squad. They hug it out before departing to make their rounds, me trailing Anderson as he runs into another longtime acquaintance.

 "My man," Roger Goodell says as he and Anderson clap backs in the Commissioner's Club, another of MetLife's many exclusive seating areas. After a brief chat, Anderson moves on to greet other patrons, but I hang around to explain to the commissioner why I'm there. It's a longish story -- and fingers crossed you'll finish! -- but the tl;dr version is that I persuaded ESPN to let me write a "Trojan Horse story": In theory, I tell Goodell, I'm using my sports world connections to make a case that Anderson, a hero of my youth, deserves to be voted in as a senior candidate to the Pro Football Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio.

 "That would make a lot of people happy," the commissioner says.

 But hidden inside that familiar sports writing trope, I continue, is a desire to answer a more profound question: Why, exactly, as a 64-year-old supposedly well-adjusted human, do I care so much about this?

 "Maybe you want to be rewarded for your loyalty," Goodell suggests.

 I respond by saying that I believe it might run deeper than that, and Goodell nods while looking at me with what seems like concern, before shaking my hand and walking away.

 So, yeah, this is a story about the Canton-worthiness of Ottis Jerome Anderson -- not to mention the psychological underpinnings of sports fandom.

 I will also be discussing "The Wizard of Oz."

 

 

 WE SHOULD PROBABLY deal with this quickly: The Hall of Fame case for Ottis Anderson is comically easy to make.

 Start with the numbers. When Anderson retired, after the 1992 season, he ranked among the NFL's all-time leaders in rushing yards (eighth), rushing touchdowns (seventh) and yards from scrimmage (ninth). He remains, somewhat astonishingly, outside Canton despite sitting squarely among -- and often ahead of -- players who are comfortably inside.

 And that's before we get to context, which is where Anderson's résumé becomes even more compelling. He wasn't just productive; he was often dominant. His rookie season in 1979 remains one of the great debuts in NFL history: 1,605 rushing yards, Offensive Rookie of the Year, first-team All-Pro. Over his first five seasons, which included the strike-shortened 1982 campaign, he amassed 6,190 rushing yards, a total that placed him among the most feared backs in the game at a time when the league was not exactly short on them. Think: Earl Campbell, Eric Dickerson, Walter Payton.

 Then there are the matters of longevity and second acts. Traded to the Giants in 1986 in what seemed like the twilight of his playing days, Anderson did not so much extend his career as reimagine it. He was named Comeback Player of the Year for the 1989 season -- the oldest running back (32) to achieve that milestone (HOF runner Marcus Allen won it four years later at 33) rushing for more than 1,000 yards. And he did so not only with a different uniform number (24), but with a completely different style.

 Early in his career, Anderson was a prototype of the modern outside back: fast, explosive, darting, capable of turning the edge and outrunning defenses. Think: Gale Sayers with size. But in New York, he became something else entirely: a punishing, between-the-tackles runner. Think: John Riggins with speed. Most players who lose a step lose their edge. Anderson changed his game and his role, and in doing so extended not just his career, but his relevance. He did not fade; he adapted.

 "I was still running a 4.5 40," he recalls, comparing that to his rookie year 4.4 time in the dash. "But Bill [Parcells] wanted me to run inside, so I ran inside."

 And then, a year after his "comeback" season -- at age 34, when most running backs are either long retired or clinging to roster spots -- Anderson delivered a steely title game performance: 102 yards, a touchdown and MVP honors in a Super Bowl XXV victory that depended greatly on his ability to grind out yards against the Buffalo Bills defense. (The Giants were starting their backup quarterback.) "The man had two totally different careers," says former Giants defensive lineman George Martin, who was a division rival and teammate of Anderson. "In one he was pretty much unstoppable -- I tried twice a year -- and in the other he was Super Bowl MVP."

 

 That performance alone should at least complicate the conversation. Hall of Fame voters have historically been susceptible to postseason moments, and few are more impressive than a Super Bowl MVP turn. When given the chance, Anderson didn't just participate in big games, he tilted them, as the kind of player coaches trusted when the game narrowed to its most consequential moments.

 And yet, for all of this -- production, longevity, postseason excellence (he also scored in Super Bowl XXI) -- Anderson remains outside the Hall, a status that becomes harder to explain the longer one looks at it. Which is why I contacted a few current and former Pro Football Hall of Fame voters, most of whom asked to speak on background. This is understandable, given the passions that HOFs can ignite, especially regarding exclusions. "Fans don't praise you for Peyton Manning getting into the Hall," says Peter King, a longtime Canton selector, now retired. "They yell at you because Roman Gabriel isn't."

 To be clear, HOF voting in professional football is now, has always been and likely always will be something of a highly subjective mess. Indeed, there's a very interesting story to write about HOF voting in pretty much every sport, in pretty much every country.

 But this is not one of those stories. Let's just all agree that members of the Canton selection committee are hamstrung by rules and procedures that can keep worthy candidates from earning enough votes. That's true for modern era players in their initial window of eligibility (19 years, beginning five years after retirement) and for seniors (25 years or more after their last season). For this reason, I didn't press any current or former voters to say if they voted for Anderson at any point over the years. But I did ask if they had any theories for his exclusion, which ranged from the specific -- "I'm not sure he was ever the best at his position in any given year" -- to the…

title: 2026 NFL season: Future Hall of Famers from all 32 teams
summary: We went roster by roster to pick out the NFL players who are on track to make the Hall of Fame one day -- and those who still have some work to do.
full_text:
How many Hall of Famers are playing in the NFL right now?

 It depends on when you're evaluating, of course. There are veterans near the end of their careers who have already proved themselves as locks to receive the game's highest honor one day, such as  Aaron Rodgers and Derrick Henry . There are players in their prime who are well on their way, such as  Justin Jefferson and Pat Surtain II . And then there are young players who haven't yet proved themselves to be Hall of Famers but could break out in the years to come, such as  Caleb Downs or Arvell Reese from the 2026 draft.

 Go back to 2002, the first year with 32 teams. There are 54 players who suited up for at least one game that season enshrined in the Hall of Fame. That list doesn't include Tom Brady (who becomes eligible in 2028) or borderline candidates such as Steve Smith and Reggie Wayne, who could earn enough votes to cross the threshold in the future. At the very least, we can use 55 Hall of Famers as our gauge, which is just under 3% of the 1,839 players who suited up for at least one game that season.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Today, I'm going through each of the league's 32 teams and attempting to identify the players who either are on track or have a realistic hope of earning gold jackets one day. This will be my estimate of who is likely to make it using historical comparables as opposed to my opinion of who should or should not be enshrined at some point. Naturally, that includes positional preferences; voters have historically loved to honor quarterbacks, running backs and receivers, but the bar is higher for linemen. I won't attempt to pick among the rookies, whom we haven't yet seen line up for an NFL snap, but I'll work with everybody else and split the most notable candidates into one of five categories:

 
 Players listed as "in" have already done enough to earn enshrinement given their existing résumé. They could retire tomorrow and make it into the Hall of Fame after they become eligible. 
 Those "on the cusp" have already done the vast majority of the work required and need only another season or two of solid play to get over the hump. As it stands, their résumé might already be enough to get in, but another successful season could push them into lock territory. 
 The "keep it up" category is for players who are performing at a Hall of Fame level but haven't done so for a long enough time to guarantee their path to enshrinement. They need to play at or near their existing level for several more seasons to have a shot. 
 Guys who have "work to do" aren't on track to make it to the Hall of Fame with their existing résumé and/or their most recent level of play. In some cases, that could be because injuries slowed their progress in 2025, or because they haven't played at a Hall-caliber level for long enough. They still have a shot, but something has to change. 
 Finally, the "missing out" category is for veterans who are at the point where they don't have the existing résumé to make it to the Hall nor the time to reestablish themselves as viable candidates. Though anything's possible, it will be a serious surprise if any of these players end up in Canton one day. They're far more likely to end up in the Hall of Very Good. 
 
 I usually start these all-32 columns with teams on the East Coast, so let's mix things up and begin out west.

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LV | LAC | LAR | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 NFC West 
 

 Arizona Cardinals 
 On the cusp: S Budda Baker 

 Baker has been stuck on some bad teams -- the Cardinals have one winning season across his nine years in the league -- but Pro Bowl voters have consistently seen him as an impactful and rangy difference-making safety. He has made eight Pro Bowls across that span. Every eligible player with at least 10 Pro Bowl appearances has been enshrined in Canton, so if Baker can earn two more, he should be a lock. One more might even be enough for the 30-year-old.

 Keep it up: TE Trey McBride 

 The invisible force field that had kept McBride out of the end zone early in his career finally lifted in 2025, as he scored 11 touchdowns, nearly doubling his total over the prior three seasons combined (six). He's not quite as explosive or elusive after the catch as Travis Kelce was in his prime or Brock Bowers has been so far as a pro, but McBride makes up that for with great hands and massive target shares.

 

 
 

 Los Angeles Rams 
 In: WR Davante Adams , Edge Myles Garrett , QB Matthew Stafford 

 I don't think I need to do much convincing here. Garrett is one of the best defenders in league history, and Adams had a five-year peak as arguably the top wide receiver in football. The case against Stafford would have been that nobody had ever really seen him as the best QB in the NFL (or close to it) in any of his first 16 years ... but after winning MVP last season, that one's out the window. He's already in the top seven for career passing yards and touchdowns, and with an MVP and a Super Bowl victory, Stafford will waltz in.

 Keep it up: WR Puka Nacua 

 Nacua already has 1,486- and 1,715-receiving yard seasons to his name by the end of his third pro campaign, which is remarkable, even given that those years are part of the 17-game era. Just for fun, the 2023 fifth-round pick is also one of the league's best blocking wideouts. The only questions are whether Nacua can stay on the field for full seasons at a time and whether there's any drop-off once Stafford is ultimately replaced by Ty Simpson .

 

 Work to do: CB Trent McDuffie , DT Kobie Turner , Edge Byron Young 

 The talented young linemen the Rams already had up front should get a boost from playing alongside Garrett. I thought Turner was the best of the bunch last season, but Young was devastating at times and parlayed his 12-sack, 29-knockdown campaign into his first Pro Bowl. I'm intrigued to see whether the Rams can afford to keep their DL standouts -- both of whom are pending free agents -- alongside Garrett for years to come.

 

 
 

 San Francisco 49ers 
 In: WR Mike Evans , RB Christian McCaffrey , OT Trent Williams 

 Evans and Williams are easy first-ballot selections. McCaffrey has struggled with injuries, but he has had multiple seasons as the best RB in the league and plays a position that the Hall is always looking to appreciate.

 On the cusp: TE George Kittle , LB Fred Warner 

 Kittle is right on the borderline of being a lock, having made seven Pro Bowls over his past eight pro campaigns before he  tore his right Achilles last postseason. I'd vote for Kittle given his dominance as a blocker and four 1,000-yard seasons, but tight ends can go underappreciated by the Hall at times. One more substantial season would push Kittle, 32, to the "lock" side of things. I'd argue the same for Warner, who had four first-team All-Pro nods over a five-year span before his own serious injury a year ago.

 Work to do: Edge Nick Bosa , QB Brock Purdy 

 Bosa has a Defensive Player of the Year award to his name, but a pair of September ACL tears have essentially cost the 2019 first-round pick two of his seven pro seasons. He needs another great season and a couple more Pro Bowl-caliber campaigns to get back on the Hall track. Purdy's efficiency has slipped since that dramatic 2023 campaign, and he has suffered meaningful injuries in three of his four pro seasons.

 Missing out: FB Kyle Juszczyk 

 Remember when I said a minute ago that every eligible player with at least 10 Pro Bowl appearances was enshrined in Canton? Well, Juszczyk will be a fascinating case to see whether that keeps up, given that he just earned his 10th consecutive Pro Bowl nod in 2025.

 Of course, while Juszczyk is a good player, it's fair to wonder whether he's racking up Pro Bowl appearances by virtue of being the most…
